title: ImageColumn: option to make the image a link (or an image display for LinkColumn)
description: ### Checklist - [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests. - [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue. ### Summary Allow a thumbnail in an `st.dataframe` `ImageColumn` to be a link that opens a URL when clicked. Today, double-clicking an image cell only shows an enlarged copy of the image. There's no way to make the image open a related page. ### Why? A common table layout is one row per item, with a thumbnail that previews a larger resource: a video clip, a detail page, or a record in another tool. The natural interaction is to click the thumbnail to open that resource. With the current column types this takes two columns: an `ImageColumn` for the preview and a `LinkColumn` (e.g. `display_text="view"`) beside it. That costs horizontal space, and users still try clicking the image first. Rendering the table as raw HTML (``) works, but you lose everything that makes `st.dataframe` worth using: sorting, row selection with `on_select`, column resizing and the toolbar. ### How? Either of these would work: 1. A `link` parameter on `ImageColumn` naming another column that holds each row's URL: ``` st.column_config.ImageColumn("Preview", link="url") ``` Clicking the image (or double-clicking, to keep single-click for row selection) opens the URL in a new tab. 2. An option on `LinkColumn` to show an image in place of `display_text`, taken from another column.It would also help if a row with no image (null) fell back to a text link in the same cell, so one column could cover rows with and without a thumbnail. ### Additional Context Related: #6894 (raw HTML cells in `st.column_config`) would also cover this, but as a general escape hatch rather than a first-class column option.

title: st.data_editor NumberColumn drops not allowed characters without any feedback - a silent data-corruption trap
description: ### Checklist - [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues. - [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue. - [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue. ### Summary When typing into a `NumberColumn` cell of `st.data_editor`, any character that the number editor does not accept is silently discarded. The most dangerous case is the decimal separator: in an app using `.` as the decimal separator, a user whose habit or OS locale uses `,` (e.g. Finland, Germany, Poland, Netherlands, Brazil) types `1,23`, the `,` is dropped and the cell commits `123` — a value 100× too large that looks perfectly plausible in the grid. There is no visual feedback at any point: the character simply does not appear, the cell is not marked as invalid, and the wrong value is returned to Python as a valid edit. In data-entry applications this is a silent data-corruption trap that is very easy to overlook. This is not a request to support other locales/separators (that is covered by #11164 / #1353). The point is more general: **the editor should never silently change what the user typed**. Rejected input should be either shown and marked invalid (like other invalid cell values) or at least clearly signalled, so the user is aware the value was not accepted as typed. A very similar silent-drop problem was recently fixed for a leading `.` (#16909, fixed in #16920), which shows the same class of issue is considered a bug. The `,` case (and any other rejected character) still behaves this way. ### Reproducible Code Example ```Python import pandas as pd import streamlit as st df = pd.DataFrame({"Item": ["I'll enter 1,23 here", "I'll enter 1.23 here"], "Factor": [0.1, 0.1]}) edited = st.data_editor( df, column_config={"Factor": st.column_config.NumberColumn("Factor", format="plain")}, hide_index=True, ) st.write(edited) ``` ### Steps To Reproduce 1. Run the app above (browser language: English, so `.` is the decimal separator). 2. Select the `Factor` cell in the first row ("I'll enter 1,23 here"), type `1,23` and press Enter. 3. Select the `Factor` cell in the second row ("I'll enter 1.23 here"), type `1.23` and press Enter. 4. Compare both cells and the values returned by `st.data_editor` (shown by `st.write(edited)` below the editor). ### Expected Behavior - Second row: `1.23` is accepted and returned as `1.23` (this works today). - First row: `1,23` must not be silently turned into another number. One of the following (in order of preference): - The typed text `1,23` stays visible in the cell editor, the cell is marked invalid (same red/invalid treatment used for other values that fail validation) and the value is not committed — the cell keeps `0.1`, or - The input is rejected with a visible message/indicator explaining that `,` is not a valid character / decimal separator. In no case should a different number than what the user typed be committed silently. It may be configurable on the column level (e.g. dropNotAllowedCharacters : bool = True), in case there are users preferring the current way. ### Current Behavior - First row: the `,` keystroke is ignored, the editor shows `123` and on Enter `123.0` is committed and returned by `st.data_editor` as a normal edit. - Second row: `1.23` is committed correctly. - The two rows now show `123` and `1.23` although the user intended the same value; no error, warning or visual indication is shown for the first row. ### Is this a regression? - [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version. ### Debug info - Streamlit version: 1.52.2 (also verified on 1.67.0) - Python version: 3.11 - Operating System: Windows 11 - Browser: Google Chrome 157.0.8103.38 (Official Build) (64-bit) - Also observed in Streamlit in Snowflake. ### Additional Information - Root cause appears to be the Glide Data Grid number overlay editor (`react-number-format` `NumericFormat`), which strips characters that do not match the configured decimal/thousand separators. Streamlit sets `thousandSeparator: ""` in `NumberColumn`, so the decimal separator is the only non-digit character accepted; everything else is dropped before Streamlit's own `validateInput` sees it. - Related issues: #16909 (same silent-drop symptom for a leading `.`, fixed in #16920), #11164 (pasting localized numbers, kept open as an enhancement), #7702, #1353 (i18n). - Current workaround is to use a `TextColumn` with a `validate` regex and convert in Python, but this loses numeric sorting and right alignment, so it is not a good general solution.

title: Let apps detect that the previous run was stopped
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

When someone stops a run, for example with `st.chat_input(submit_mode="stop")` while a reply streams, the app gets no signal that the run was stopped. Chat apps want to show "You stopped this response" with a **Try again** button, so they have to infer the stop from their own history: the last message is the user's, and there's no new prompt.

### Why?

- **Inference is fragile.** The "last message is the user's" check also matches other states, such as a run that crashed or a message the app appended without replying. Every chat app reimplements the check.
- **The note appears late.** The stop ends the run before the app can draw anything, so the stopped note and retry button only appear on the next rerun, after the user interacts again.
- **Partial output is lost.** Whatever `st.write_stream` had streamed before the stop never reaches the app, so it can't keep the partial answer in history.

### How?

Some options:

1. **A flag on the next run**, for example `st.context.previous_run_stopped`, so the app can render the stopped state without guessing.
2. **An `on_stop` callback on `st.chat_input`**, which runs on the stop, before the rerun, and can record the state.
3. **A rerun after a stop**, optionally, so the app can draw the stopped state right away instead of waiting for the next interaction.

A way for `st.write_stream` to hand back what it streamed before the stop would also help keep partial answers.

### Additional Context

The current workaround is documented in the agent skill's `chat-ui.md` and used in the `chat-analyst` template ([#18064](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/18064)) and the [agent app demo](https://github.com/streamlit/demos/tree/main/agent-app).

title: Show the chat input's stop button for replies started by other widgets
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

With `st.chat_input(submit_mode="stop")`, the send button turns into a stop button only for runs that the chat input itself started. Chat apps commonly start replies from other widgets too, such as suggestion pills on the start screen or follow-up pills under the last answer. Those replies stream just as long, but the input keeps its send arrow, so the only way to stop them is the toolbar's **Stop**.

### Why?

From the user's point of view, a suggestion or follow-up is the same as typing the prompt. The reply looks and behaves the same, so the input should offer the same stop button. Today this is by design: the [submit_mode spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-04-08-chat-input-submit-mode/product-spec.md) says the behavior "only affects the specific `st.chat_input` instance that triggered the current script run", and `ChatInput.tsx` shows the stop button only while its own `submittedRunScope` is set.

### How?

Some options:

1. **Built-in suggestions on `st.chat_input`**, as requested in [#8318](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8318). Picks would be submissions of the chat input, so they would get `submit_mode` for free, and the pills would also clear themselves (see [#16375](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/16375)).
2. **A way to submit the chat input programmatically**, for example from a widget callback, so the next run counts as started by the chat input.
3. **An option to apply `submit_mode` to any run** while the chat input is on the page, for example `submit_mode="stop"` plus a flag that covers runs started by other widgets.

Option 1 covers the common case with the least API.

### Additional Context

Found while building the [agent app demo](https://github.com/streamlit/demos/tree/main/agent-app) and the `chat-analyst` template in [#18064](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/18064). [#11854](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11854) introduced the stop button.

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

When a widget is written directly into an `st.empty()` slot, and a later run creates the same slot but writes nothing to it, the widget stays on screen until that run finishes. It isn't even marked stale: it stays fully interactive and keeps its selection. If the widget is wrapped in `slot.container()` instead, it disappears as soon as the run reaches the slot.

This matters for chat apps that hide suggestion or follow-up pills while the next reply streams. Without the container workaround, the picked pill stays highlighted above the streaming reply.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import time

import streamlit as st

mode = st.query_params.get("mode", "direct")
slot = st.empty()

if st.session_state.get("picked"):
    st.write(f"Picked {st.session_state.picked}. Working for 3 seconds...")
    time.sleep(3)
elif mode == "direct":
    slot.pills("Follow up", ["A", "B"], key="picked")
else:
    with slot.container():
        st.pills("Follow up", ["A", "B"], key="picked")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app and open it with `?mode=direct`.
2. Click the **A** pill.
3. While "Working for 3 seconds..." shows, look at the pills.
4. Repeat with `?mode=container`.

### Expected Behavior

In both modes, the pills disappear as soon as the run reaches `slot = st.empty()`, because that run leaves the slot empty.

### Current Behavior

- `?mode=direct`: the pills stay visible and interactive, with **A** still selected, until the run finishes.
- `?mode=container`: the pills disappear right away.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.67.0 (`develop` at 8a34d3dbd4)
- Python version: 3.15.2
- Operating System: macOS
- Browser: Chromium (Playwright)

### Additional Information

Related, but not the same case: [#2395](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/2395) (`.empty()` clears a widget only at the end of the script, closed), [#12069](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12069) (`st.empty` does not clear removed elements), and [#10126](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/10126) (removing stale elements in LLM apps).

Found while building the follow-up pills of the [agent app demo](https://github.com/streamlit/demos/tree/main/agent-app) and the `chat-analyst` template in [#18064](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/18064), which both use the container workaround.

title: st.dataframe with a pixel height draws over elements below it after resizing with the drag handle
description: :robot: _AI text below_ :robot: ### Checklist - [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues. - [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue. - [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue. ### Summary When `st.dataframe` gets a fixed pixel `height`, you can still drag its bottom-right resize handle past that height, up to the full table height. The element container stays at the configured height and doesn't clip its content, so the resized grid draws over every element below it (buttons, text, other elements). Those elements don't move down. `height="stretch"` already handles this case (its comment says "dragging grows the parent, as with `height="auto"`"). The integer-height path doesn't. ### Reproducible Code Example ```python # repro.py import pandas as pd import streamlit as st st.title("Resizable dataframe overlap") jobs = pd.DataFrame( { "job_id": range(1000, 1060), "status": ["done", "error", "queued"] * 20, "description": ["Mock processing job"] * 60, } ) # A fixed pixel height (8 rows here). Drag the bottom-right corner of the table downwards. st.dataframe(jobs, height=300, width="stretch") st.button("Button below the table") st.write("Text below the table. After resizing, the table paints over this.") ``` ### Steps To Reproduce 1. `streamlit run repro.py` 2. Hover over the bottom-right corner of the table until the resize cursor shows. 3. Drag the corner down about 300px and let go. ### Expected Behavior The element container grows with the table, and the button and text move down below it. That's what happens with `height="auto"` and `height="stretch"`. ### Current Behavior The table grows from 300px to 595px, but the element container stays 300px tall. The button and text don't move, so the table covers them. I measured this with Playwright: after the drag, the table's bottom edge is at y=780 and the button's top edge is still at y=501. Screenshots, before and after applying the CSS workaround described below: **Before (1.67.0 as-is, after dragging):** the button and text are under the table. **After (with the workaround below, same drag):** the button and text move below the table. ### Why it happens (1.67.0) 1. **The table can grow past its configured pixel height.** With an integer height, `initialHeight` is the configured height, but `maxHeight` is the full content height, so the drag can go well past the configured height: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/89f84a3a8abf0ca28226ad902c945c854e4a763a/frontend/lib/src/components/widgets/DataFrame/hooks/useTableSizer.ts#L197-L201 The `bottomRight` handle is enabled and uses that `maxHeight`: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/89f84a3a8abf0ca28226ad902c945c854e4a763a/frontend/lib/src/components/widgets/DataFrame/DataFrame.tsx#L1122-L1147 2. **The element container is fixed to the pixel height.** For `DimensionType.PIXEL`, the layout sets `height: ${pixels}px` (with `overflow: auto`): https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/89f84a3a8abf0ca28226ad902c945c854e4a763a/frontend/lib/src/components/core/Layout/useLayoutStyles.ts#L387-L389 3. **The container's overflow is then set to `visible`.** Dataframes use `LARGE_OVERFLOW_VISIBLE`, which overrides `overflow` to `visible`: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/89f84a3a8abf0ca28226ad902c945c854e4a763a/frontend/lib/src/components/core/Block/ElementNodeRenderer.tsx#L704-L722 https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/89f84a3a8abf0ca28226ad902c945c854e4a763a/frontend/lib/src/components/core/Block/ElementContainerConfig.ts#L152-L155 So the container keeps its pixel height and doesn't clip, and the resized grid draws outside it. Compare the stretch path, which handles exactly this case: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/89f84a3a8abf0ca28226ad902c945c854e4a763a/frontend/lib/src/components/widgets/DataFrame/hooks/useTableSizer.ts#L163-L178 ### Possible fix For dataframes with a pixel height, have the container's height follow the resizable height (`height: auto`, with the pixel value used only as the grid's initial size). Another option is to cap `maxHeight` at the configured height, but that would remove resizing for these tables. ### Workaround CSS that lets the element container follow the grid. With this applied, the button moves to y=796, just below the table: ```python st.html( '" ) ``` ### Is this a regression? - [x] Yes, this used to work in a previous version. ### Debug info - Streamlit version: 1.67.0 - Python version: 3.13.16 - Operating System: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS - Browser: Google Chrome 157.0.8103.50 ### Additional Information The source links above are pinned to the `1.67.0` tag. As of today, the same code is still on `develop` in `useTableSizer.ts` and `useLayoutStyles.ts`.

title: Split long-format data into series in st.echarts_chart
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

`st.echarts_chart` has no equivalent of the built-in charts' `color=<column>` or Altair's `color` encoding. To draw one series per category from long-format data (one row per x value and category), every app has to pivot the dataframe to one column per category and write one series per column. Add a way to split one long-format `dataset.source` into series, in a stable order, without a manual pivot.

### Why?

Long-format data is what most queries return, and the built-in charts and Altair take it directly. With `st.echarts_chart`, apps (and the coding agents writing them) pivot it by hand:

```python
wide = df.pivot_table(index="date", columns="endpoint", values="requests").reset_index()
st.echarts_chart(
    {
        "dataset": {"source": wide},
        "xAxis": {"type": "time"},
        "yAxis": {},
        "series": [
            {"type": "line", "name": endpoint, "encode": {"x": "date", "y": endpoint}}
            for endpoint in wide.columns[1:]
        ],
    }
)
```

The pivot looks harmless, but it's where the bugs come from. Converting the bundled skill templates from Altair to ECharts (#18006) hit these:

- **Order changes silently.** `pivot_table` sorts its index and columns. String category labels such as `"Apr 01"` sort before `"Jan 01"`, so a day-of-year axis came out alphabetical. Keeping the order needs an ordered `Categorical` dtype or a manual `reindex`.
- **Colors don't match across charts.** ECharts assigns palette colors in series order, and in data order for pies. A donut fed by `value_counts()` (most common first) and stacked bars fed by a pivot (alphabetical) gave the same category different colors. Altair avoids this with one shared, sorted category scale. Keeping colors stable when filters remove categories is #17837. This issue is about the reshaping that makes the order fragile in the first place.
- **Duplicates aggregate silently.** `pivot_table` averages duplicate (x, category) rows by default, so a wrong `aggfunc` changes the chart without an error.
- **Boilerplate.** Every grouped chart needs the pivot, a `reset_index()` (the index isn't sent), and a list comprehension over the new columns.

ECharts' own alternative is one `filter` transform dataset per group, with a series per dataset via `datasetIndex`. It keeps the data long, but it's longer than the pivot, and the app still has to list the groups in Python.

### How?

Options, roughly from smallest to largest. This needs design exploration before committing to one:

1. **Series expansion in the backend.** A Streamlit-specific series key, for example `"splitBy": "endpoint"` (name open), that Streamlit expands into one series per distinct value. Each expanded series is named after its value and reads a filtered view of the same `dataset.source`. The order follows the column's categorical order if it has one, otherwise first appearance, with an option for sorted order. The data stays one Arrow table, so **Show data** and the agent API keep reporting a single dataframe.
2. **A Python helper** that builds the wide dataframe and the series list from long data in a defined order, for example a function in `streamlit` that returns `(source, series)`. It's simpler to ship, but it doesn't keep the data long.
3. **Docs only.** Document the pivot pitfalls and the `filter` transform pattern in the `st.echarts_chart` docstring and the embedded skill. The skill's `charts.md` already covers the pivot and `filter` patterns, so this alone doesn't remove the bugs.

Combined with palette-slot references from #17837, option 1 would give `st.echarts_chart` the same "color by column" behavior the built-in charts have, while staying JSON-only.

### Additional Context

- Found while converting the `developing-with-streamlit` skill's dashboard templates to `st.echarts_chart` (#18006), which makes ECharts the recommended chart command.
- Related: #17837 (stable category colors across charts), #17888 (number formats for ECharts axis labels).

title: Clear cached query results of a single st.connection after writes
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a way to clear the cached results of `conn.query()` for a single connection, so a writeback app can show fresh data right after it writes. Today the only built-in option is `st.cache_data.clear()`, which also clears every other cached function in the app.

### Why?

Apps that act, such as approval queues, triage tools, and planning input, read with `conn.query()` and write with `conn.session` or a cursor. After a write, the next `query()` call can still return the old rows from its cache.

- Without a `ttl`, cached results never expire, so the page keeps showing the pre-write data.
- A short `ttl` only narrows the window, and costs a query on every expiry.
- `ttl=0` disables caching altogether.
- `st.cache_data.clear()` works, but it also drops unrelated caches, such as expensive model or reference-data loads.

The workaround is to skip `conn.query()` and write your own cached readers, then clear each one after a write:

```python
@st.cache_data(ttl="5m")
def load_proposals() -> pd.DataFrame:
    with conn.engine.connect() as db:
        return pd.read_sql(text("SELECT * FROM proposals"), db)

def record(decision):
    with conn.session as session:
        session.execute(text("UPDATE proposals SET status = :status WHERE id = :id"), ...)
        session.commit()
    load_proposals.clear()
```

That defeats the purpose of `query()`, whose docstring presents it as the cached, retrying way to read.

### How?

Add a method that clears the cached `query()` results of that connection only, for example:

```python
conn = st.connection("orders_db", type="sql")
proposals = conn.query("SELECT * FROM proposals WHERE status = 'pending'", ttl="5m")

with conn.session as session:
    session.execute(text("UPDATE proposals SET status = 'approved' WHERE id = :id"), {"id": po})
    session.commit()

conn.clear_query_cache()  # Next conn.query(...) reads fresh rows
```

Notes for the implementation:

- `SQLConnection.query()` and `BaseSnowflakeConnection.query()` each build a `cache_data` function whose `__qualname__` includes the connection name and the `ttl`. So one connection can have several caches, one per `ttl` value used. Clearing should cover all of them for that connection, and leave other connections and other cached functions alone.
- Snowflake caches query results in the connection's `scope()`, so session-scoped results stay private. Clearing should respect that scope: it should clear the current session's entries for a session-scoped connection, not other sessions'.
- `reset()` is a natural place to document it next to, but it should stay separate: `reset()` reinitializes the underlying connection, and doesn't touch cached results.
- Alternatives worth weighing: `conn.query.clear()`, which is harder because `query` is a bound method, or a `clear_cache: bool` argument on `query()`.

### Additional Context

This came up while building the `act-review-queue` template for the embedded `developing-with-streamlit` agent skill (#18008). It uses the custom-reader workaround above. Writeback is one of the three use cases Streamlit's positioning leads with ("apps that act"), so a one-line cache clear after a write would make that pattern simpler for both people and coding agents.

title: Session-scoped resources: release them when the session ends, and allow st.connection(scope="session")
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Make session-scoped resources live as long as the session they belong to:

1. Release `@st.cache_resource(scope="session")` entries, including session-scoped connections, when the session ends, not on every WebSocket disconnect.
2. Let `st.connection` create a session-scoped connection of a built-in type, for example `st.connection("db", type="sql", url=..., scope="session")`.

### Why?

Public apps that write data need state that belongs to one visitor. The `apps-that-act` demo in [streamlit/demos](https://github.com/streamlit/demos/tree/main/apps-that-act) gives each browser session its own SQLite database, so one visitor's approvals never change what others see.

`@st.cache_resource(scope="session", on_release=...)` looks like the right tool, but two gaps get in the way:

- **Session-scoped resources are released on every disconnect.** `WebsocketSessionManager.disconnect_session` calls `session.clear_session_caches()` before it saves a resumable session for reconnect (`runtime/websocket_session_manager.py`). After a network blip, the session resumes with its Session State, but its session-scoped resources are gone. An `on_release` that deletes the visitor's database file would drop their work while Session State still points at it. The `cache_resource` docstring already warns that an unstable connection can repopulate the cache several times in one session.
- **Built-in connections can't be session-scoped.** `SQLConnection.scope()` returns `"global"`, and the scope is fixed per connection class. A session-scoped SQL connection needs a subclass that overrides `scope()`, so most apps don't discover it.

Because of both gaps, the demo works around it: a unique `st.connection` name per session, `max_entries` and `ttl` to bound the cache, and a sweep that deletes database files older than a day.

### How?

- **Release at session end.** `AppSession.shutdown()` already clears session caches. Releasing session-scoped entries only there would match the lifetime of Session State. If some apps rely on prompt release at disconnect, for example to free GPU memory, this could be opt-in, e.g. `release_on="disconnect" | "session_end"`.
- **A `scope` parameter on `st.connection`.** It would default to the connection class's `scope()`, and `"session"` would use the same per-session cache that caller's-rights Snowflake connections already use. A class that requires session scope should still reject `"global"`.

With both in place, a per-session resource with cleanup is a few lines, and this use case doesn't need a separate session-end hook:

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import streamlit as st


@st.cache_resource(scope="session", on_release=lambda path: path.unlink(missing_ok=True))
def session_database() -> Path:
    path = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "demo.db"
    seed(path)  # Fill the visitor's copy of the demo data
    return path


conn = st.connection(
    "demo", type="sql", url=f"sqlite:///{session_database()}", scope="session"
)
```

### Additional Context

- Related: #7688 asks for generic session start and shutdown hooks. This request is narrower: make the existing session-scoped resources match the session's lifetime, and expose session scope for built-in connections.
- Current workaround: [`apps-that-act/utils/store.py`](https://github.com/streamlit/demos/blob/main/apps-that-act/utils/store.py).

title: `st.date_input` accepts reversed date ranges from query parameters
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce the problem.

### Summary

When `st.date_input` is used in range mode with `bind="query-params"`, a URL containing two valid dates in reverse order is accepted as-is. The widget returns the end date before the start date, despite the date range being invalid.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
from datetime import date
import streamlit as st

st.date_input(
    "Date range",
    value=(date(2025, 3, 1), date(2025, 3, 15)),
    key="period",
    bind="query-params",
)
```

Open the app with the `period` query parameter containing `2025-03-15` followed by `2025-03-01` (for example, `?period=2025-03-15&period=2025-03-01`).

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the example above.
2. Open the app with `period` set to two in-bounds date values in descending order.
3. Read the value returned by `st.date_input`.

### Expected Behavior

Invalid reversed query-parameter ranges should not be exposed as a reversed date range. The widget should reject the malformed range and fall back to its configured default, consistent with how it handles invalid and out-of-bounds query-parameter values.

### Current Behavior

`DateInputSerde.deserialize` parses both dates and returns them in the original order. It validates that the dates are individually within bounds, but does not check that the start date is less than or equal to the end date.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: Current `develop` checkout
- Python version: Not verified
- Operating System: Not verified
- Browser: Not verified

### Additional Information

The existing date-input serde tests cover ordered ranges and out-of-bounds values, but not reversed ranges.

title: Unify the default height of charts, maps, and dataframes
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Charts, maps, and dataframes each use a different default height: 350px for Vega-based charts and `st.echarts_chart`, up to 400px for `st.dataframe`, 450px for `st.plotly_chart`, and 500px for `st.map` and `st.pydeck_chart`. Placed side by side, they only line up if the author passes the same `height` to each. This request proposes one shared default height of **400px** (`25rem` at the default font size) for all of them. The frontend would resolve it from a single theme token.

### Why?

Dashboards place charts, maps, and tables next to each other in `st.columns`, `st.grid`, and cards. With today's defaults, a line chart next to a Plotly chart is 100px shorter, and a map next to a dataframe is 100px taller, so the bottoms of the row don't line up. The workaround is to pass the same integer `height` (or `height="stretch"`) to every element in the row. Our own examples do this: the `st.grid` docstring passes `height=220` to a line chart, a bar chart, and a dataframe, and the embedded skill's `dashboards.md` passes `height=260`. The embedded skill also tells agents to use Vega or ECharts for ordinary charts and Plotly for 3D and scientific charts, so agent-built dashboards mix libraries by design.

The defaults also scale differently with `theme.baseFontSize`. Vega charts and dataframes use rem values from the frontend theme. ECharts (350), Plotly (450), and maps (500) send fixed pixel values from Python. With a 14px base font, a line chart is 306px and a dataframe is 350px, but an ECharts chart stays at 350px.

Current defaults on `develop`:

| Element | Default height | Source | Scales with base font size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `st.line_chart`, `st.area_chart`, `st.bar_chart`, `st.scatter_chart`, `st.altair_chart`, `st.vega_lite_chart` | 350px | `theme.sizes.defaultChartHeight` (`21.875rem`), used as Vega-Lite `continuousHeight` | Yes |
| `st.echarts_chart` | 350px | `_DEFAULT_CONTENT_HEIGHT` in `echarts_chart.py` (copies the Vega token) | No |
| `st.dataframe`, `st.data_editor` (`height="auto"`) | Up to 400px (header + ~10 rows) | `defaultTableHeight` (`25rem`) in `DataFrame/hooks/useCustomTheme.ts` | Yes |
| `st.plotly_chart` | 450px | Plotly.js default; `_resolve_content_height` in `plotly_chart.py`, `DEFAULT_PLOTLY_HEIGHT` in `PlotlyChart.tsx` | No |

title: Drag-and-drop cell reordering for `st.grid`, saved in localStorage
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Let viewers rearrange the cells of an `st.grid` with drag and drop. If the grid has a `key`, save the order in the browser's `localStorage` so the layout is still there after a reload or a later visit.

### Why?

`st.grid` is designed for metric walls, card galleries, and dashboard panels. On dashboards, different viewers often care about different panels. Today the order is fixed by the script, so the only way to personalize it is to build settings widgets and store preferences in a database, which is a lot of work for a small win.

Dashboard tools like Grafana, Datadog, and Power BI, and layout libraries like [React Grid Layout](https://github.com/react-grid-layout/react-grid-layout), let users move panels around. The `st.grid` product spec (`specs/2026-05-14-grid-layout`) listed "draggable, resizable, or user-persisted layouts" as out of scope for the first version, so this request proposes the reordering part as a follow-up.

### How?

Add an opt-in parameter:

```python
grid = st.grid(3, reorderable=True, key="kpis")
grid.metric("Revenue", "$1.2M", "+8%", border=True)
grid.metric("Pipeline", "$4.8M", "+12%", border=True)
grid.metric("Conversion", "12.4%", "+1.1%", border=True)
```

Proposed behavior:

- **Drag handle:** A handle appears when the pointer is over a cell, or when the cell has keyboard focus. Only the handle starts a drag, so charts, dataframes, and inputs inside the cell work as usual.
- **Client-side only:** Reordering doesn't trigger a rerun, and Python doesn't see the new order, the same way the sidebar width works (the sidebar width is also kept in `localStorage`). The order survives reruns within the session.
- **Persistence:** If `key` is set, the order is saved in `localStorage`, scoped to the app, page, and grid key. Without a `key`, the order lasts only for the current session (or, alternatively, `reorderable=True` requires a `key`; see open questions).
- **Changes in the script:** If the script adds cells, they go at the end of the saved order. If it removes cells, they are dropped from the saved order. If the grid's structure changes too much (for example, a different number of cells), the saved order is discarded.
- **Reset:** A way to go back to the order in the script, for example a "Reset layout" entry in the app menu or a toolbar action on hover.
- **Accessibility:** Keyboard reordering (pick up with Space/Enter, move with arrow keys, drop with Space/Enter) with screen-reader announcements. The DOM order should change along with the visual order, unlike CSS `order` or `dense`, so keyboard and screen-reader order match what users see.
- **Spans:** Cells that span several columns (`grid.cell(column_span=2)`) move as one unit and keep their span.

Open questions:

1. **Cell identity:** Matching saved positions to cells by index breaks when cells are conditional or come from a loop over changing data. Should `grid.cell()` accept a `key` for a stable identity, with index-based matching as the fallback?
2. **Without a `key`:** Should reordering keep the order for the session only, or require a `key`?
3. **Reading the order in Python:** Is there a later need to read the order back (for example, through `st.session_state[key]`), or to set it from Python to save it per user on the server? That would need a widget-like value and is probably a separate follow-up.
4. **Name:** `reorderable`, `draggable`, or `sortable`?

Out of scope for this request: resizing cells, moving cells between grids, and server-side persistence.

### Additional Context

- `st.grid` feature request: #11101
- Related drag-and-drop request: #6700 (`st.multiselect`)
- Related discussion on client-side state: #17242
- Existing `localStorage` example: sidebar width (`frontend/app/src/components/Sidebar/Sidebar.tsx`)

title: API consistency: parameter order of date_input versus slider and number_input
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the existing issues for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Could Streamlit clarify the intended parameter-order convention for widgets that accept a value and minimum/maximum bounds? In 1.67.0, `st.date_input` places `value` before the bounds, while `st.slider` and `st.number_input` place it after them. This is an API consistency discussion, not a report of incorrect widget behavior.

### Why?

The leading parameters are:

```python
st.date_input(label, value, min_value, max_value, ...)
st.slider(label, min_value, max_value, value, ...)
st.number_input(label, min_value, max_value, value, ...)
```

Switching between these widgets requires remembering two positional conventions for similar concepts. This also comes up when writing application wrappers that present a consistent interface.

### How?

Is there a historical or design reason for this difference? It would be helpful to establish a convention for future APIs and consider how existing APIs could align if a backward-compatible path becomes available.

I am not proposing an immediate reorder: that would change the meaning of existing positional calls. Using explicit keyword arguments is a workable approach today.

### Additional Context

Compared the implementation signatures in Streamlit 1.67.0:

- [date_input](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.67.0/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/time_widgets.py#L1847)
- [slider](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.67.0/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/slider.py#L529)
- [number_input](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.67.0/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/number_input.py#L353)

title: Support column header alignment in st.dataframe / st.data_editor
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

`st.column_config` columns accept `alignment` ("left" / "center" / "right") for cell content, but column headers are always left-aligned. Please let headers be aligned too, either by following the column's `alignment` or through a separate header alignment option.


### Why?

Centring a column's cells leaves its header pinned to the left edge, so on wide columns the header no longer sits over its data. That looks broken in business dashboards, where centred numeric columns are a common house style.

There's no workaround: the grid is canvas-rendered, so custom CSS can't reach the header text, and pandas `Styler` header styles are ignored (#6958). The only option today is to drop `st.dataframe` for an HTML table and lose sorting, resizing, search and virtualisation.

Theming already covers the header's *colours* (`dataframeHeaderBackgroundColor`, `dataframeHeaderTextColor`), so alignment is the main header property that still can't be controlled.

Minimal example (Streamlit 1.67.0):

```python
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

df = pd.DataFrame({"Name": ["Alpha", "Bravo", "Charlie"], "Count": [10, 20, 30], "Score": [1.5, 2.5, 3.5]})
st.dataframe(
    df,
    hide_index=True,
    column_config={c: st.column_config.Column(c, alignment="center", width="medium") for c in df.columns},
)
# Cells are centred; headers stay left-aligned.
```


### How?

Either of these would work:

1. **Header follows the column:** when `alignment` is set on a column, apply it to the header as well. This is the simplest option and matches what most people expect from "align this column".
2. **Explicit parameter:** add `header_alignment: Literal["left", "center", "right"] | None = None` to `st.column_config.Column` and its subclasses. `None` keeps today's behaviour or follows `alignment`.

An optional theme-level default (e.g. `[theme] dataframeHeaderAlignment = "center"`) would avoid repeating it for every column, the same way the header colour options work today.


### Additional Context

- Related: #12106 (cell/content alignment, closed), #11110 (`alignment="center"` not applied to cells; fixed April 2025), #6958 (header styling from pandas `Styler` isn't kept, open).
- Use case: internal dashboards running on Streamlit in Snowflake (container runtime). Header alignment would only reach those apps through a Streamlit release, so a built-in option matters more than a workaround.

title: st.popover stays open and floats when its tab or expander is hidden
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

Opening an `st.popover` and then hiding its trigger leaves the popover body on screen. Switching away from the tab that contains it, or collapsing the expander that contains it, pins the body to the top-left corner of the page instead of closing it.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import streamlit as st

tab_a, tab_b = st.tabs(["A", "B"])
with tab_a:
    with st.popover("Popover in tab"):
        st.write("Popover content")

with st.expander("Expander", expanded=True):
    with st.popover("Popover in expander"):
        st.write("Popover content")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app and open "Popover in tab".
2. Switch to tab B.
3. Go back to tab A and open "Popover in expander".
4. Collapse the expander.

### Expected Behavior

Hiding the trigger closes the popover. Showing the tab or expander again leaves it closed.

### Current Behavior

The popover body stays open and floats at the top-left of the page (about x=8, y=4). Showing the tab or expander again does not put it back on its button.

The body is rendered in a portal on `document.body`, outside the tab or expander. Hiding the trigger does not unmount it. With a hidden anchor, Floating UI's `shift` middleware pins the body to the viewport corner. A click on another tab does not reach the popover's document click listener, because that click is stopped before it bubbles.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.65.0 (develop, before the fix)
- Python version:
- Operating System: macOS
- Browser:

### Additional Information

Fix: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17477

title: Streamlit number formats for st.echarts_chart axis labels
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

`st.echarts_chart` axis labels can't use Streamlit's number formats. `axisLabel.formatter` accepts only ECharts string templates such as `"{value} MB"`, so a byte axis shows `10,000,000` instead of `9.5 MiB`, and a fraction axis shows `0.05` instead of `5%`. Accept the same number formats that `tooltip.valueFormatter` already supports (`"bytes"`, `"compact"`, `"percent"`, `"dollar"`, printf strings) in `axisLabel.formatter`.

### Why?

Moving an internal dashboard app (about 85 charts) to `st.echarts_chart`, axis labels were the second biggest formatting gap after tooltips:

- **Bundle size chart:** the y axis reads `2,000,000 … 12,000,000` (bytes) while its tooltip, using `"valueFormatter": "bytes"`, reads `9.5 MiB`. The axis and the tooltip disagree.
- **Rates stored as fractions:** a template can append a unit (`"{value}%"`) but can't multiply by 100, so the axis reads `0.05%`.
- **Large counts or currency:** there's no compact (`1.2M`) or currency format without a JavaScript callback, which `st.echarts_chart` doesn't support.

The workaround is to rescale the data in pandas (for example, divide by 1,048,576 and append " MiB" in a template). That changes the values in tooltips, in the **Show data** table, and in the agent API's data, and it doesn't pick a unit per tick the way `"bytes"` does.

### How?

Treat a string `axisLabel.formatter` as a Streamlit number format when it is one, the same rule `tooltip.valueFormatter` uses today:

```python
st.echarts_chart(
    {
        "dataset": {"source": df},
        "xAxis": {"type": "time"},
        "yAxis": {"type": "value", "axisLabel": {"formatter": "bytes"}},
        "series": [{"type": "bar", "encode": {"x": "date", "y": "size"}}],
        "tooltip": {"trigger": "axis", "valueFormatter": "bytes"},
    }
)
```

- **Detection.** A named format (`"bytes"`, `"compact"`, `"percent"`, ...) or a printf string with a placeholder (`"%.1f s"`) that has no `{...}` template placeholder. Templates such as `"{value} MB"` or `"{value}%"` keep ECharts' meaning.
- **Backward compatibility.** In ECharts, a string without `{value}` prints literally on every tick, so no working spec uses `"bytes"` or `"%.1f"` as an axis formatter. Existing charts wouldn't change.
- **Validation.** As with `valueFormatter`, the frontend would ignore a malformed printf string, and Python would log a warning.

Open questions:

- Which other label formatters should accept the formats? Candidates are `axisPointer.label.formatter`, series `label.formatter` (bar and point labels show raw values like `10545470.237731934` today), and `visualMap` / `dataZoom` labels.
- Should value axes under the Streamlit theme shorten long numbers by default, like the theme already does in tooltips?
- Time axes already have ECharts' `{yyyy}`/`{MM}` templates. Do they need date formats here, or only numbers?

### Additional Context

- Product spec: `specs/2026-07-06-echarts-chart/product-spec.md`, "Tooltip formatting". It lists "number formats for axis labels" as not included, and "Tradeoffs" says axis labels still need pre-formatted strings.
- Related: [#17128](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/17128) (JavaScript callback support, the JavaScript route to the same result).

title: Per-field number and date formats in st.echarts_chart tooltips
description:
### Checklist - [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests. - [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue. ### Summary `st.echarts_chart` tooltips can't format individual fields without JavaScript. `{@column}` placeholders in a tooltip `formatter` template insert raw values, and `tooltip.valueFormatter` applies one number format to every value of a series. Support per-field number and date formats in tooltips, so a tooltip can show `9.5 MiB`, `3.8%`, and `Jan 03` side by side. ### Why? Moving an internal dashboard app (about 85 charts) to `st.echarts_chart`, the biggest source of friction was tooltips with extra fields, such as a commit SHA, a date, and a size. Every coding agent working on it hit this independently. - **Templates insert raw values.** `"formatter": "{@sha}
size: {@size}
date: {@date}"` renders `size: 11000000.5` and `date: 2026-01-02T00:00:00.000`. `valueFormatter` doesn't apply to template placeholders, and the docstring says so: "Values are inserted as escaped text without a number format". - **One format per series.** `valueFormatter: "percent"` formats every numeric value of the series as a percent, so a tooltip can't show a percentage next to a byte size or a count. - **No date formats.** Printf-style formats and the named number formats don't cover dates, so dates in templates show as full ISO strings. The workaround was to round columns or add pre-formatted string columns to the dataframe. Those extra columns also show up in the chart's **Show data** table and in the agent API's data. A separate fix ([#17883](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17883)) labels each `encode.tooltip` field in the default tooltip and shows dataframe datetimes readably there. Per-field formats in the default tooltip and in templates are still missing. ### How? These are the options considered so far, from smallest to most expressive. They aren't mutually exclusive. **A. Apply the existing formatting to placeholders.** `{@column}` values would use the tooltip's `valueFormatter` when set, and the Streamlit theme's number shortening and date formatting otherwise. It's the smallest change and needs no new syntax, but there is still only one number format per tooltip. **B. A format per placeholder.** For example `{@size|bytes}`, `{@pct|%.1f%%}`, or `{@date|MMM DD}`: ```python "tooltip": {"formatter": "{@sha}
{@size|bytes} · {@date|MMM DD}"} ``` - Number formats would be the ones `st.metric(format=...)` and `valueFormatter` already accept. Date formats could reuse the momentJS formats of `st.column_config.DatetimeColumn(format=...)`. - It's flexible, but it's syntax only Streamlit understands. The original product spec rejected a similar `{@[2]:compact}` suffix for that reason. - `|` already means rich text in ECharts label templates (`{style|text}`), so the separator needs care. **C. A per-field format mapping.** ```python "tooltip": {"valueFormatter": {"size": "bytes", "pct": "percent", "date": "MMM DD"}} ``` - This would apply in both the default tooltip and templates, and keeps templates portable. - ECharts calls `valueFormatter` without saying which dimension a value belongs to, so the frontend would have to match values to fields through `encode.tooltip`. That makes it more work than A or B. It lists "per-dimension formats" and "date/time formats for tooltip values" as not included. - Related: [#17128](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/17128) (JavaScript callback support, the JavaScript route to the same result).

title: The `Runtime` loop keeps the last flushed session alive through its `active_session_info` loop variable
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

`Runtime._loop_coroutine` iterates `for active_session_info in self._session_mgr.list_active_sessions():` and never clears the loop variable. While the coroutine is suspended between flushes, the variable keeps a strong reference to the `ActiveSessionInfo` (and through it the `AppSession` and its client) of the last session it flushed. After that session disconnects, is dropped from session storage, and becomes otherwise unreachable, it stays alive and is not shut down until the next flush cycle rebinds the variable, which does not happen while no connected session produces messages.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
# app.py: the same diagnostic app as in #17860.
import gc
import threading
import time
import types

import streamlit as st
from streamlit.runtime import Runtime
from streamlit.runtime.app_session import AppSession
from streamlit.runtime.scriptrunner import get_script_run_ctx


def holders(session):
    """Describe what keeps an AppSession alive, looking through the SessionInfo wrapper."""
    mgr = Runtime.instance()._session_mgr
    storage_data = mgr._session_storage._cache._data
    active_by_id = mgr._active_session_info_by_id
    found = []
    for wrapper in gc.get_referrers(session):
        if type(wrapper).__name__ not in ("SessionInfo", "ActiveSessionInfo"):
            continue
        for ref in gc.get_referrers(wrapper):
            if ref is storage_data:
                found.append("MemorySessionStorage._cache._data")
            elif ref is active_by_id:
                found.append("WebsocketSessionManager._active_session_info_by_id")
            elif isinstance(ref, types.CoroutineType):
                found.append(f"coroutine {ref.cr_code.co_name}")
            elif isinstance(ref, dict):
                found.append(f"other dict ({type(ref).__name__})")
    return found


@st.cache_resource
def monitor():
    def report():
        while True:
            time.sleep(2)
            rt = Runtime.instance()
            gc.collect()
            alive = [o for o in gc.get_objects() if isinstance(o, AppSession)]
            print(
                f"[monitor] {time.strftime('%T')}"
                f" managed={len(rt._session_mgr.list_sessions())}"
                f" alive_AppSession={len(alive)}"
                f" media_sessions={len(rt.media_file_mgr._files_by_session_and_coord)}"
                f" alive={ {s.id[:8]: (s._state.name, holders(s)) for s in alive} }",
                flush=True,
            )
            del alive

    threading.Thread(target=report, daemon=True).start()


sid = get_script_run_ctx().session_id
monitor()

# A 1x1 PNG, so each session holds a media-file reference until shutdown() clears it.
st.image(bytes.fromhex(
    "89504e470d0a1a0a0000000d4948445200000001000000010806000000"
    "1f15c4890000000d49444154789c63f8cfc0f01f0005000201a5d2a1c600"
    "00000049454e44ae426082"
))
st.write("session", sid)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app with a short TTL:
   ```
   streamlit run app.py --server.disconnectedSessionTTL 10
   ```
2. Open tab U and leave it idle.
3. Open tab V, let its script run finish, and close it.
4. Wait longer than the TTL, then close tab U. Its disconnect writes to session storage, which reaps V's expired entry.
5. Watch the `[monitor]` lines.

### Expected Behavior

Once V is disconnected and dropped from session storage, nothing in the runtime references it, so it is garbage collected (and shut down by `AppSession.__del__`).

### Current Behavior

Monitor output (Streamlit 1.65.0, TTL 10 s, abridged). `59ff13eb` is U, `80c382f8` is V. V closed at 15:54:24, U at 15:54:39.

```
[monitor] 15:54:26 managed=2 alive_AppSession=2 media_sessions=2 alive={'59ff13eb': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['WebsocketSessionManager._active_session_info_by_id']), '80c382f8': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['coroutine _loop_coroutine', 'MemorySessionStorage._cache._data'])}
[monitor] 15:54:41 managed=1 alive_AppSession=2 media_sessions=2 alive={'80c382f8': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['coroutine _loop_coroutine']), '59ff13eb': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['MemorySessionStorage._cache._data'])}
[monitor] 15:54:51 managed=0 alive_AppSession=2 media_sessions=2 alive={'80c382f8': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['coroutine _loop_coroutine']), '59ff13eb': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['MemorySessionStorage._cache._data'])}
```

From 15:54:41 on, V is no longer in session storage and the only reference to it is the suspended `_loop_coroutine` frame. It keeps its media file reference and is not shut down. It stays alive until another flush cycle runs, that is, until some connected session enqueues a message.

The loop is at [runtime.py#L802-L821](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/runtime.py#L802-L821) on `develop` (61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a) and at [`runtime.py` L714-728](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/ff22743ac9b00f19f7416d6b2cf4be19b0fa37ea/lib/streamlit/runtime/runtime.py#L714-L728) on 1.65.0. After the loop, the coroutine suspends in `asyncio.wait()` on `need_send_data` ([L830-L838](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/runtime.py#L830-L838)) or, once no session is connected, on `has_connection` ([L783-L791](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/runtime.py#L783-L791)), with `active_session_info` (and `msg_list`, `msg`) still bound.

Deleting the variables after the loop (`del active_session_info`, or moving the flush into a helper so the references go out of scope) would release the reference.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.65.0 (loop unchanged on `develop` at 61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a)
- Python version: 3.12.14
- Operating System: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS
- Browser: Chromium 151 (headless)

### Additional Information

The effect is bounded to one session at a time, but it matters for anything tied to the session's lifetime: memory held in its session state, its media files, and resources that a component releases on session shutdown. It also makes weakref- or `gc`-based leak checks report one surviving `AppSession` after all tabs are closed.

title: Disconnected sessions are not shut down when their `disconnectedSessionTTL` expires
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

When a disconnected session's `server.disconnectedSessionTTL` expires, `MemorySessionStorage` stops returning it, but nothing calls `AppSession.shutdown()` on it. The expired entry stays in the storage's `TTLCache` until some later write (the next disconnect of any session) reaps it, and even then the session is only shut down by `AppSession.__del__` if nothing else references it. Until then the session keeps its media file references, uploaded files, dataframe sources, and script-thread event loop, and it can no longer be reached by `Runtime.close_session()` or by the shutdown loop in `Runtime.stop()`.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
# app.py
import gc
import threading
import time
import types

import streamlit as st
from streamlit.runtime import Runtime
from streamlit.runtime.app_session import AppSession
from streamlit.runtime.scriptrunner import get_script_run_ctx


def holders(session):
    """Describe what keeps an AppSession alive, looking through the SessionInfo wrapper."""
    mgr = Runtime.instance()._session_mgr
    storage_data = mgr._session_storage._cache._data
    active_by_id = mgr._active_session_info_by_id
    found = []
    for wrapper in gc.get_referrers(session):
        if type(wrapper).__name__ not in ("SessionInfo", "ActiveSessionInfo"):
            continue
        for ref in gc.get_referrers(wrapper):
            if ref is storage_data:
                found.append("MemorySessionStorage._cache._data")
            elif ref is active_by_id:
                found.append("WebsocketSessionManager._active_session_info_by_id")
            elif isinstance(ref, types.CoroutineType):
                found.append(f"coroutine {ref.cr_code.co_name}")
            elif isinstance(ref, dict):
                found.append(f"other dict ({type(ref).__name__})")
    return found


@st.cache_resource
def monitor():
    def report():
        while True:
            time.sleep(2)
            rt = Runtime.instance()
            gc.collect()
            alive = [o for o in gc.get_objects() if isinstance(o, AppSession)]
            print(
                f"[monitor] {time.strftime('%T')}"
                f" managed={len(rt._session_mgr.list_sessions())}"
                f" alive_AppSession={len(alive)}"
                f" media_sessions={len(rt.media_file_mgr._files_by_session_and_coord)}"
                f" alive={ {s.id[:8]: (s._state.name, holders(s)) for s in alive} }",
                flush=True,
            )
            del alive

    threading.Thread(target=report, daemon=True).start()


sid = get_script_run_ctx().session_id
monitor()

# A 1x1 PNG, so each session holds a media-file reference until shutdown() clears it.
st.image(bytes.fromhex(
    "89504e470d0a1a0a0000000d4948445200000001000000010806000000"
    "1f15c4890000000d49444154789c63f8cfc0f01f0005000201a5d2a1c600"
    "00000049454e44ae426082"
))
st.write("session", sid)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app with a short TTL:
   ```
   streamlit run app.py --server.disconnectedSessionTTL 10
   ```
2. Open the app in two or more browser tabs and close them all. (With a single tab, that session is also held by the issue reported in #17861; the earlier tabs show this issue alone.)
3. Wait well past the TTL (30 seconds or more) and watch the `[monitor]` lines.
4. Optionally, open and close one more tab. Its disconnect is a write to session storage, which reaps the expired entries; the `[monitor]` lines then show that this, not expiry, is what finally releases them.

### Expected Behavior

When a stored session expires (or is evicted because the storage is at `maxsize`), it is shut down the same way `WebsocketSessionManager.close_session()` shuts down a stored session: `AppSession.shutdown()` runs, so the session's media file references, uploaded files, dataframe sources, and script-thread event loop are released at expiry, without waiting for another session to disconnect or for garbage collection.

### Current Behavior

Monitor output from the steps above (Streamlit 1.65.0, TTL 10 s, abridged). The three tabs closed at 15:53:24.

```
[monitor] 15:53:27 managed=3 alive_AppSession=3 media_sessions=3 alive={'7bbf1984': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['coroutine _loop_coroutine', 'MemorySessionStorage._cache._data']), '77b13f38': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['MemorySessionStorage._cache._data']), '8c46c9bc': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['MemorySessionStorage._cache._data'])}
[monitor] 15:53:35 managed=0 alive_AppSession=3 media_sessions=3 alive={'7bbf1984': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['coroutine _loop_coroutine', 'MemorySessionStorage._cache._data']), '77b13f38': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['MemorySessionStorage._cache._data']), '8c46c9bc': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['MemorySessionStorage._cache._data'])}
[monitor] 15:53:53 managed=0 alive_AppSession=3 media_sessions=3 alive={'7bbf1984': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['coroutine _loop_coroutine', 'MemorySessionStorage._cache._data']), '77b13f38': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['MemorySessionStorage._cache._data']), '8c46c9bc': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['MemorySessionStorage._cache._data'])}
                                   (one more tab opens at 15:53:55 and closes at 15:53:57)
[monitor] 15:53:58 managed=1 alive_AppSession=1 media_sessions=1 alive={'2d34defb': ('APP_NOT_RUNNING', ['coroutine _loop_coroutine', 'MemorySessionStorage._cache._data'])}
```

- From 15:53:35 on, the session manager no longer lists the three sessions (`managed=0`), yet all three `AppSession` objects stay alive with their media file references (`media_sessions=3`) and a state other than `SHUTDOWN_REQUESTED`. What holds them is the storage's `TTLCache` (`MemorySessionStorage._cache._data`).
- They stay that way until another session disconnects at 15:53:57. Its `MemorySessionStorage.save()` reaps the expired entries, the `AppSession` objects become unreachable, and `AppSession.__del__` finally calls `shutdown()`. In an app that gets no further disconnects, the expired sessions stay alive indefinitely.
- One of the three is also referenced by `Runtime._loop_coroutine`; that reference is reported separately (see the last item under Additional Information).

The relevant code (the same on 1.65.0 and on `develop` at 61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a):

- `MemorySessionStorage` is a plain `TTLCache` with no removal hook ([memory_session_storage.py#L62-L64](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/memory_session_storage.py#L62-L64)). Expired entries "are only actually removed by a write, by `expire()`, or by a length query" ([ttl_cache.py#L24-L27](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/caching/ttl_cache.py#L24-L27)), and removal does not call `shutdown()`.
- `WebsocketSessionManager.disconnect_session()` stops the script and saves the session into storage ([websocket_session_manager.py#L315-L364](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/websocket_session_manager.py#L315-L364)). `shutdown()` is only called from `close_session()` ([websocket_session_manager.py#L375-L400](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/websocket_session_manager.py#L375-L400)), and for a stored session only when `self._session_storage.get(session_id)` still returns it ([L394](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/websocket_session_manager.py#L394)), which it does not once the TTL has passed.
- `Runtime.close_session()` looks the session up with `get_session_info()` first ([runtime.py#L574-L576](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/runtime.py#L574-L576)), so an expired session cannot be closed by id either.
- On `Runtime.stop()`, the loop shuts down only `list_sessions()` ([runtime.py#L851-L855](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/runtime.py#L851-L855)), which excludes expired entries.
- The only remaining path is `AppSession.__del__` → `shutdown()` ([app_session.py#L299-L301](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/app_session.py#L299-L301)), which depends on reaping and on nothing else referencing the session.

On 1.65.0 the corresponding lines are [`memory_session_storage.py` L62-64](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/ff22743ac9b00f19f7416d6b2cf4be19b0fa37ea/lib/streamlit/runtime/memory_session_storage.py#L62-L64), `websocket_session_manager.py` [L238-262](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/ff22743ac9b00f19f7416d6b2cf4be19b0fa37ea/lib/streamlit/runtime/websocket_session_manager.py#L238-L262) (`disconnect_session`) and [L273-297](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/ff22743ac9b00f19f7416d6b2cf4be19b0fa37ea/lib/streamlit/runtime/websocket_session_manager.py#L273-L297) (`close_session`), `runtime.py` [L486-489](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/ff22743ac9b00f19f7416d6b2cf4be19b0fa37ea/lib/streamlit/runtime/runtime.py#L486-L489) and [L760-765](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/ff22743ac9b00f19f7416d6b2cf4be19b0fa37ea/lib/streamlit/runtime/runtime.py#L760-L765), and [`app_session.py` L279-281](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/ff22743ac9b00f19f7416d6b2cf4be19b0fa37ea/lib/streamlit/runtime/app_session.py#L279-L281).

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.65.0 (code paths unchanged on `develop` at 61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a)
- Python version: 3.12.14
- Operating System: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS
- Browser: Chromium 151 (headless)

### Additional Information

- #6166 covers the same lazy expiry from the user-facing side. The [comment there](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6166#issuecomment-1442576663) describes the deferred cleanup as expected because `TTLCache` only removes expired entries "when the cache is next mutated". This report is about the consequence for resources: until that mutation, and afterwards whenever something else holds a reference, `shutdown()` never runs. Code that holds a reference to the `AppSession` while waiting for it to reach `SHUTDOWN_REQUESTED` (for example, a component that tears down its own resources on session shutdown) keeps it alive, so `__del__` never runs and the session is never shut down.
- A comment in `WebsocketSessionManager.__init__` already anticipates the case of "a disconnected session [...] later evicted from storage without an explicit close" ([websocket_session_manager.py#L127-L132](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/websocket_session_manager.py#L127-L132)).
- On `develop`, `TTLCache` accepts an `on_remove` callback ([ttl_cache.py#L60](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/61258800c1ba561b2b4a175aba41b95bbd37bd9a/lib/streamlit/runtime/caching/ttl_cache.py#L60)), which `MemorySessionStorage` does not pass. Expiry would still only be detected on the next write or length query, so prompt release would also need something to call `expire()` periodically.
- A related reference that keeps one disconnected session alive regardless of storage is reported separately (the `active_session_info` loop variable in `Runtime._loop_coroutine`).

title: Efficient re-scan of module paths upon `sys.modules` changes
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

When `sys.modules` changes, [`update_watched_modules()`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L276) rebuilds the path set for every loaded module rather than for the names that were added, so importing one module re-resolves all of them.
For a better performance removing the bottleneck, it should scan only the difference, which the method already has in hand.

### Why?

The rebuild runs inline on the event loop, from `AppSession._handle_scriptrunner_event_on_event_loop` ([`:843`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/runtime/app_session.py#L843), [`:867`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/runtime/app_session.py#L867)), so nothing is served while it runs. Each path goes through [`realpath()` plus `_is_valid_path()`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L348), which [stats it](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L353), and the cost therefore follows the size of the dependency tree and the latency of the filesystem rather than the size of the change.

[#4491](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/4491) fixed the case where `sys.modules` is unchanged, by [caching the set of names](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L280). What remains is the cache miss, which any lazy import causes, and in an app that loads models on demand those keep happening long after startup.

The work beyond the new names is discarded anyway: [`_file_is_new()`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L266) is `filepath not in self._watched_modules`, so already-watched paths are rejected right after being stat'd. Removals are not handled either way, since [`_deregister_watcher()`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L255) is only called from [the pages path](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.66.1/lib/streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py#L119).

Measured on an app with the environment on a network filesystem, polling `/_stcore/health` ten times a second (median 1.3 ms) while one module is imported mid-session:

| event | latency |
| --- | --- |
| scan after the startup import of 3000 modules | 580 ms |
| scan after the later import of **one** module | 550 ms |
| ~950 modules loaded instead of ~3950, one module imported | 229 ms |

One module costs what three thousand do, and the figure follows the total rather than the change. On a local disk the same scan is far cheaper, so a small app will not notice it.


### How?

Resolve paths only for `set(sys.modules) - self._cached_sys_modules`, which the method computes already as part of its cache check. No change to where the work runs and no new concurrency. The only behavior given up is noticing that an already-imported module mutated its own `__path__` in place without its name changing.

Moving the sweep off the event loop would bound the worst case regardless of tree size or filesystem latency, but running it there after a script run is presumably what keeps watcher state off a second thread, and [#4491](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/4491) already noted multi-threading concerns here. With an incremental scan the remaining window is one module's paths, so that may not be worth the risk.

### Additional Context

This came out of our real use case, where we do suffer from it. The app runs for hours streaming audio and video to the browser, carries `torch` and `transformers` (1700 to 3900 loaded modules), and its environment sits on a network filesystem. Models load on demand, so `sys.modules` keeps changing mid-session, and each rescan stopped the server sending anything for **0.3 to 3.7 seconds**, long enough for the browser to conceal all audio and freeze video. A watchdog dumping thread stacks mid-stall put six of eight dumps in this path:

```
File "streamlit/runtime/app_session.py", line 714 in _handle_scriptrunner_event_on_event_loop
File "streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py", line 272 in update_watched_modules
File "streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py", line 340 in get_module_paths
File "streamlit/watcher/local_sources_watcher.py", line 346 in _is_valid_path
File "<frozen genericpath>", line 30 in isfile
```

(1.58.0 line numbers, where it was captured; verified unchanged in 1.66.1.) Scanning that dependency tree (1682 paths) in a plain Python process took 340 ms to 13666 ms depending on attribute cache state, the high reading seen once and not reproducible on demand. We now disable file watching to keep sessions usable.

A standalone app that shows the stall, needing no third party packages:

```python
import pathlib
import sys
import tempfile
import time

import streamlit as st

MODULES = 3000  # set to 0 for the control
# Outside the script folder on purpose: files under it are watched
# individually, which is a separate cost and not what this reproduces.
PKG = pathlib.Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "fake_deps_pkg" / "fake_deps"


@st.cache_resource
def build_and_import() -> int:
    PKG.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    (PKG / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    for i in range(MODULES):
        (PKG / f"mod{i}.py").write_text(f"value = {i}\n")
    sys.path.insert(0, str(PKG.parent))
    for i in range(MODULES):
        __import__(f"{PKG.name}.mod{i}")
    return len(sys.modules)


st.write(f"{build_and_import()} modules loaded at startup, {len(sys.modules)} now")


# A button click would do as well; this just triggers the one rerun unattended.
@st.fragment(run_every="3s")
def import_one_more() -> None:
    if st.session_state.get("imported"):
        st.write("idle")
        return
    st.session_state["imported"] = True
    (PKG / "extra.py").write_text("")
    __import__(f"{PKG.name}.extra")
    st.write(f"imported ONE module at {time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}")


import_one_more()
```

Run it, open it in a browser so a session exists, and poll an endpoint the event loop serves while the single extra module is imported a few seconds in:

```sh
while true; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{time_total}\n" http://localhost:8501/_stcore/health
  sleep 0.1
done
```

Verified against 1.66.1 by reading the source at that tag, after measuring on 1.58.0. Python 3.12.2, Linux 5.15.0.

title: Add `icon` parameter to `st.selectbox`
description:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add an `icon` parameter to `st.selectbox` that shows an emoji or Material icon inside the input field, to the left of the selected value. `st.text_input` (#10761) and `st.number_input` (#10711) already support this, which came from #8787.

### Why?

An icon hints at what the field is for (a globe for a country, a person for an assignee, a calendar for a reporting period) and lets a selectbox line up visually with text and number inputs that already have icons in the same form.

Today the only workaround is prefixing every option with an emoji via `format_func`. That repeats the icon in every dropdown row, changes the displayed value, and can't use Material icons (#12151).

### How?

Match the existing `icon` parameter on `st.text_input` and `st.number_input`:

```python
country = st.selectbox("Country", countries, icon=":material/public:")
assignee = st.selectbox("Assignee", people, icon="👤", placeholder="Pick someone")
```

- `icon: str | None = None`. Accepts a single-character emoji, `":material/icon_name:"`, or `"spinner"`, validated with `validate_icon_or_emoji` and documented with the same docstring as the other inputs.
- The icon renders at the start of the input field, before the selected value or placeholder. It stays visible while the user types to filter options, with `accept_new_options=True`, and when the widget is disabled.
- Size, spacing, and color match the start icon of `st.text_input` / `st.number_input` (`StyledStartEnhancer`), so the three widgets align when stacked.
- As with the other inputs, `icon` is part of the widget ID only when no `key` is set.

### Additional Context

- Original request for input icons: #8787.
- Related but separate: icons and Markdown inside option labels (#12151, #7466).
- `st.multiselect`, `st.date_input`, and `st.time_input` could get the same parameter later; this issue covers `st.selectbox` only.
