A possible correction is to return positive infinity when `intra_disp == 0.0` and `extra_disp > 0.0`, while preserving the existing `1.0` behavior when both dispersions are zero.

I have tested a small local correction against the development version. It resolves the reproduced behavior, and a new regression test fails before the correction and passes afterward.

The clustering metrics test suite reports 189 passed and 61 skipped tests. The skipped tests require optional Array API libraries or settings, so I haven't checked whether the fix works with all supported backends.

I would be happy to receive maintainer feedback on whether returning infinity is the preferred behavior and on the proposed approach and test coverage before opening a PR

### Introduce yourself

i have been contributing to [skore](https://github.com/probabl-ai/skore) (https://github.com/probabl-ai/skore/pulls?q=is%3Apr+state%3Aopen+author%3Adirekkakkar319-ops) for a few months, and I also contribute to [pgmpy](https://github.com/pgmpy/pgmpy)

In pgmpy `BaseCasualDiscovery` we use `validate_data()` for data validation . As currently we are working for implementing narwhals in pgmpy we tried to do the validation using just the `validate_data()` , but when we tested is on the nw.dataframe of pandas then we got the error
```python
    if backend == "pandas_nullable":
        df = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.Series([1, 2, 1, 2], dtype="Int64"), "b": [2, 1, 2, 1]})
        data = nw.from_native(df)
        expected_a_dtype = "Int64"
    ..
    unmigrated = UnmigratedDiscovery()
    res = unmigrated.fit(data)
```

Related links
* https://github.com/pgmpy/enhancement_proposals/pull/19
* https://github.com/pgmpy/pgmpy/pull/3659

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

in `validation.py` we do:
```python
        # Note that array may be a narhwals.DataFrame backed by a pandas.DataFrame.
        df_pandas = array_df.to_native()
```

but further in the code after few lines when we do 
```python
    if pandas_requires_conversion:
        # pandas dataframe requires conversion earlier to handle extension dtypes with
        # nans
        # Use the original dtype for conversion if dtype is None
        new_dtype = dtype_orig if dtype is None else dtype
```

title: Add e-means clustering (EMeans)
description:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a data scientist working as Sr. Quantitative analyst for the Los Angeles Dodgers. Most of my professional work lives in-house, but I'd like to give back to the broader community so I've decided spend more of my free time pursuing open source projects. SKL was a staple of my (previous) life as a scientist, and of course plays a role in my career outside of academia. 

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I'd like to get KMeans-quality centers in a handful of passes over the data. In the runs below KMeans needed 19 to 229 iterations, and MiniBatchKMeans is cheap per pass but ends with worse inertia. Usage would be `EMeans(n_clusters=256, n_epochs=5).fit(X)`, with the rest of the KMeans interface (predict, transform, score, sparse input, sample_weight).

### Describe your proposed solution

e-means is a mini-batch k-means published in November 2026 by Bessa et al. at Meta FAIR: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09501. Each center is an exponential moving average of the points assigned to it, and the learning rate decays along a cosine. The batch size and the initial learning rate are computed from scaling laws that the authors fitted, so the user only chooses the number of epochs. Their reference code is in faiss, https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/tree/main/contrib/e_means, and their benchmark scripts are in https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/tree/main/benchs/e_means.

The paper reports that e-means reaches the loss of 25 Lloyd iterations in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs on embedding datasets.

I have a prototype built on scikit-learn's existing k-means Cython code. On five datasets on my laptop it fit 1.8 to 17 times faster than KMeans, and its inertia was between 0.7% lower and 0.5% higher. The 17x case was 200,000 points in 64 dimensions with 256 clusters: 0.56 s against 9.5 s. All five datasets are synthetic or small, so these numbers need a proper benchmark behind them.

From the same initial centers and random numbers, the prototype gives the same centers as faiss's NumpyEmeans at every step, except where two centers tie at float32 precision.

The paper is from this month, so this is nowhere near the 3 years and 200 citations in the FAQ. I'm opening this because the FAQ also allows a clear-cut improvement on a widely used method, and I'd like to know if you think this qualifies.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

MiniBatchKMeans was slower than the prototype in the same runs and finished 0.3% to 2.8% above KMeans in inertia. https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/30051 also changes the learning rate of mini-batch k-means. If this doesn't belong in core I can publish it as a scikit-learn-contrib package.

### Additional context

The prototype comes with tests and docs, and I can open a draft PR once this is triaged. It doesn't copy any faiss code. I used AI assistance (Claude Code) to write it but have reviewed the changes thoroughly and believe in the work.

title: DummyClassifier predicts incorrect labels for sparse targets with nonconsecutive classes
description:

> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. ### Introduce yourself

I'm currently pursuing a Master's degree in Computer Science and Engineering at Instituto Superior Técnico, specializing in Artificial Intelligence and Distributed Systems. I previously completed a Bachelor's degree in Engineering Physics and have experience with ML research within and outside Physics.

I'm currently using scikit-learn in a Data Science course. Separately, I'm interested in understanding and improving the correctness and also reliability of ML software. While trying to learn and investigating the implementation of `DummyClassifier`, I identified a discrepancy between predictions made with dense and sparse target representations and reproduced it locally.

Although I haven't encountered this issue in my coursework, I believe it's relevant enough to fix, since baseline classifiers should produce correct predictions regardless of the supported representation of their target data

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When DummyClassifier is fitted on a sparse target matrix with nonconsecutive integer class labels, the most_frequent and prior strategies can predict an incorrect class label.

For example, with training labels [4, 4, 4, 0, 1], the majority class is 4. The classifier correctly predicts 4 when fitted on a dense target array, but predicts 2 when fitted on an equivalent CSC sparse target matrix.

The value 2 is not even present among the training labels!

This is a silent correctness problem rather than an exception. It means that a baseline classifier can return an invalid class label depending on the representation of the targets. This matters when checking classification baselines because predictions should preserve the original class labels

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```
import numpy as np
from scipy import sparse
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier

X = np.zeros((5, 1))
y = np.array([4, 4, 4, 0, 1])
y_sparse = sparse.csc_matrix(y.reshape(-1, 1))

for strategy in ("most_frequent", "prior"):
    dense_clf = DummyClassifier(strategy=strategy).fit(X, y)
    sparse_clf = DummyClassifier(strategy=strategy).fit(X, y_sparse)

    print(f"{strategy}:")
    print("  dense:", dense_clf.predict(X))
    print("  sparse:", sparse_clf.predict(X).toarray().ravel())
```

### Expected Results

Both strategies should predict class label 4 for every sample, regardless of whether the training targets are represented as a dense NumPy array or a sparse CSC matrix:

```
most_frequent:
  dense: [4 4 4 4 4]
  sparse: [4 4 4 4 4]
prior:
  dense: [4 4 4 4 4]
  sparse: [4 4 4 4 4]
```

### Actual Results

The dense classifiers return the majority class label 4, but the sparse classifiers return 2.

```
most_frequent:
  dense: [4 4 4 4 4]
  sparse: [2 2 2 2 2]
prior:
  dense: [4 4 4 4 4]
  sparse: [2 2 2 2 2]
```

No exception or warning is raised

For example, when the classes are [0, 1, 4], the highest class probability is at index 2, but the corresponding class label is 4

A possible correction is to map the index back to the actual class label through classes_ before generating sparse predictions.

I have tested a small local correction that resolves the reproduced behavior for both most_frequent and prior. I would also include a regression test with nonconsecutive class labels to prevent this from happening again.

I have not yet run the full upstream test suite. I would welcome maintainer feedback on the proposed approach and test coverage before opening a PR

title: confusion_matrix silently accepts duplicate labels and returns a misleading matrix
description:
### Introduce yourself

Hello, I'm a Master's student in Computer Science, specializing in Artificial Intelligence and the Internet of Things

My background includes machine learning and computer vision, particularly image classification. I use scikit-learn's evaluation tools to understand model performance, and I'm interested in making classification metrics more reliable and easier to interpret.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When the `labels` argument contains duplicate values, `sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix` returns a matrix without raising an error or warning.

For example, passing `labels=[0, 0, 1, 2]` for a three-class classification problem produces a 4×4 matrix instead of the expected 3×3 matrix.

The duplicate label introduces an additional row and column. Counts for class `0` are assigned to the last matching position, while the first occurrence has an all-zero row and column.

This matters in multiclass image classification, where confusion matrices are used to assess performance across categories. If duplicate labels are accidentally supplied, the resulting matrix can be misleading, particularly when it is used for visualization or exported for reporting.

I suggest validating that the `labels` argument contains unique values and raising an informative `ValueError` if duplicates are detected.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce


import sklearn
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

print(sklearn.__version__)

y_true = [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2]
y_pred = [0, 1, 1, 0, 2, 2]
labels = [0, 0, 1, 2]

cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=labels)

print(cm)
print(cm.shape)


### Expected Results

The function should reject duplicate class labels with an informative error message, for example:

```text
ValueError: The 'labels' parameter must contain unique class labels.
Duplicate label found: 0.
```

Alternatively, a warning could be issued, although raising an error would help prevent misleading evaluation results.

### Actual Results

Reproduced in Google Colab using scikit-learn 1.9.1.

```text
1.9.1
[[0 0 0 0]
 [0 2 0 0]
 [0 0 1 1]
 [0 0 1 1]]
(4, 4)
```

No error or warning was observed. The first occurrence of label `0` produces an all-zero row and column, while the second occurrence receives the counts for that class.

title: BUG: `partial_fit` returns `None` in `MultiOutputRegressor` and `BernoulliRBM`, contradicting its documented `Returns self`
description:
### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for classical ML pipelines, and a good part of that is the incremental-learning API: we feed data in batches and chain the calls, e.g. `est.partial_fit(X_batch, y_batch).predict(X_batch)`. I found the two cases below while auditing every `partial_fit` implementation in the library against its own documented `Returns` section.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`partial_fit` is documented (and, in this library, uniformly implemented) as returning `self`, so that it can be chained like `fit`. Two implementations return `None` instead, while their own docstrings still promise `self`:

1. `MultiOutputRegressor.partial_fit` — the override just calls the parent's implementation without returning it (`sklearn/multioutput.py:430`), even though its docstring documents `self` (`sklearn/multioutput.py:425-428`). Its sibling `MultiOutputClassifier` inherits `_MultiOutputEstimator.partial_fit`, which does `return self` (`sklearn/multioutput.py:203`) — so within the same class hierarchy one of the two subclasses returns the estimator and the other returns `None`.
2. `BernoulliRBM.partial_fit` — ends after `self._fit(...)` (`sklearn/neural_network/_rbm.py:310`), although its docstring documents `self` (`sklearn/neural_network/_rbm.py:282-285`) and `BernoulliRBM.fit` does `return self` (`sklearn/neural_network/_rbm.py:437`).

**User-facing impact.** The documented chaining idiom raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ...`, which does not point at the real problem. Worse, the natural incremental-training loop

```python
est = MultiOutputRegressor(SGDRegressor())
for X_batch, y_batch in batches:
    est = est.partial_fit(X_batch, y_batch)   # silently becomes None
```

silently replaces the estimator with `None` and only fails at the *next* batch, far from the cause. This is especially confusing for people who write the same loop generically over several estimators, since it works for every other incremental estimator in scikit-learn (including `MultiOutputClassifier`) and fails only for these two.

**Scope of the audit.** I checked all 24 `partial_fit` definitions under `sklearn/`: 21 end with `return self`, one (`CategoricalNB`) returns the result of `super().partial_fit(...)`, and these two are the only ones that return `None`.

**Why the test suite does not catch it.** `sklearn/tests/test_multioutput.py:78` (`test_multi_target_regression_partial_fit`) does exercise `MultiOutputRegressor.partial_fit`, but it only checks the predictions afterwards, never the return value, so a `None` return passes unnoticed.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np

from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier, SGDRegressor
from sklearn.multioutput import MultiOutputClassifier, MultiOutputRegressor
from sklearn.neural_network import BernoulliRBM

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = rng.rand(20, 4)
y = rng.rand(20, 2)

# 1. both return None
print(MultiOutputRegressor(SGDRegressor(random_state=0)).partial_fit(X, y))
print(BernoulliRBM(n_components=3, random_state=0).partial_fit(X))

# 2. the classifier sibling returns the estimator, as documented
print(
    MultiOutputClassifier(SGDClassifier(random_state=0)).partial_fit(
        X, (y > 0.5).astype(int), classes=[np.array([0, 1])] * 2
    )
)

# 3. the documented chaining idiom breaks
MultiOutputRegressor(SGDRegressor(random_state=0)).partial_fit(X, y).predict(X)
BernoulliRBM(n_components=3, random_state=0).partial_fit(X).transform(X)
```

### Expected Results

Both calls return the fitted estimator, i.e. `partial_fit(...) is est`, and the two chained expressions of step 3 return an array of shape `(20, 2)` and `(20, 3)` respectively — consistent with the docstrings and with `fit`.

### Actual Results

```
None
None
MultiOutputClassifier(estimator=SGDClassifier(random_state=0))
```

```python-traceback
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'predict'
```

```python-traceback
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'transform'
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.12 (main, Feb  4 2026, 00:05:32) [Clang 21.1.4 ]
   machine: macOS-14.5-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0 (editable build of main @ 6e37063)
          pip: 26.3
        numpy: 2.5.4
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: 3.3.1
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.8.0

Built with OpenMP: False
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would like to open the PR for this once the issue is triaged — no PR before that, as requested.

**Root cause.** Both are overrides/rewrites of an existing `partial_fit` that dropped the return value, while the docstring was copied over unchanged:

- `sklearn/multioutput.py:430`: `super().partial_fit(...)` → needs `return super().partial_fit(...)`. The parent already returns the right object, so no logic is duplicated.
- `sklearn/neural_network/_rbm.py:310`: the method ends after `self._fit(...)` → needs `return self`.

**Proposed fix (2 lines of production code).** Exactly the two changes above, plus one non-regression test per module. Each test also asserts the sibling that already works (`MultiOutputClassifier.partial_fit` / `BernoulliRBM.fit`), so that the failing assertion is attributable to the fix and not to the test scaffolding.

**Evidence from my local experiment** (branch `fix/partial-fit-return-self` on `main @ 6e37063`):

- on `main`, the two new tests fail with exactly `assert None is MultiOutputRegressor(estimator=SGDRegressor(max_iter=5, random_state=0))` and `assert None is BernoulliRBM(n_components=16, random_state=0)`;
- with the fix, the two target files go from `96 passed` (base) to `98 passed`;
- `pytest sklearn/tests/test_common.py -k "BernoulliRBM or MultiOutputRegressor"`: 106 passed, 13 skipped, 2 xfailed;
- `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` (0.12.2, the version pinned in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`) clean on the four touched files.

The change is strictly backward compatible for callers: `None` is not a usable value, and no code in `sklearn/` consumes the return value of either method.

---

title: BUG: FrozenEstimator.set_params returns None instead of self, breaking the documented set_params(...).predict(...) chaining idiom
description:
### Introduce yourself

I maintain scikit-learn-based pipelines for tabular work and have been contributing small fixes upstream. This report came out of an AI-assisted audit of the newer `sklearn.frozen` module while looking for contract inconsistencies between `FrozenEstimator` overrides and the `BaseEstimator` API they shadow; I reproduced and verified everything below myself on a source build of `main`, and the proposed fix + regression test are ready locally.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`FrozenEstimator.set_params` documents that it returns `self`, and `BaseEstimator.set_params` documents the same thing — with the chaining idiom spelled out in its docstring:

* `sklearn/base.py:205` — `>>> estimator.set_params(param=3).fit(X, y).predict(X)`
* `sklearn/frozen/_frozen.py:129-133` — `Returns ------- self : FrozenEstimator  This estimator.`

The implementation (`sklearn/frozen/_frozen.py:118`) never returns anything: it mutates `self.estimator`, may raise `ValueError` for inner parameters, and then falls off the end of the function, so `set_params` returns `None`.

User-facing impact: any chained call on a frozen estimator breaks. `FrozenEstimator(clf).set_params(estimator=other_clf).predict(X)` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'predict'` instead of predicting with `other_clf`. You have to split the call into two statements, which is exactly the thing the `BaseEstimator` contract exists to avoid — the idiom appears ~25 times inside scikit-learn's own test suite (`sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_coordinate_descent.py`, `sklearn/preprocessing/tests/test_encoders.py`, `sklearn/ensemble/tests/test_voting.py`, …) and in user-facing docstring examples (`sklearn/pipeline.py:207`).

Why it slipped through: `FrozenEstimator` deliberately overrides `set_params` (it rejects `estimator__*` kwargs), and the sibling override `fit` does `return self` correctly, so only this one override is affected. The existing test `test_frozen_params` (`sklearn/frozen/tests/test_frozen.py:202`) exercises the state mutation but never checks the return value — a test asymmetry with the rest of the estimator API, where `set_params` returning `self` is relied on everywhere.

Note that this is not a `BaseEstimator.set_params` regression: the parent implementation still returns `self` (asserted as a control in the reproducer below), so the difference is attributable to the override alone.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.frozen import FrozenEstimator
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = make_classification(random_state=0)
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
other_clf = LogisticRegression(C=0.1).fit(X, y)

# Control: the parent implementation returns `self`, so chaining works.
assert clf.set_params(C=2.0) is clf

frozen = FrozenEstimator(clf)
print(frozen.set_params(estimator=other_clf))  # None
frozen.set_params(estimator=other_clf).predict(X)
```

### Expected Results

`set_params` returns the `FrozenEstimator` instance itself (not the inner estimator), as documented in both its own docstring and `BaseEstimator.set_params`, so that

```python
frozen.set_params(estimator=other_clf).predict(X)
```

predicts with `other_clf` and returns an array of shape `(n_samples,)`.

### Actual Results

```python-traceback
None
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 14, in <module>
    frozen.set_params(estimator=other_clf).predict(X)
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'predict'
```

### Proposed fix

One line: `return self` at the end of `FrozenEstimator.set_params` (after the existing `ValueError` raise for `estimator__*` keys), leaving all current behaviour — including the `ValueError` for inner parameters — untouched, plus a regression test that pins the return value with a control assertion on the parent implementation.

I verified this locally against a source build of `main` @ `6e37063` (macOS arm64, Python 3.13.12):

* Red on clean `main` with the new test in place, for the claimed reason — `assert None is FrozenEstimator(estimator=LogisticRegression(C=0.1))`, while the `BaseEstimator` control assertion passes both before and after:
  ```
  sklearn/frozen/tests/test_frozen.py:233: AssertionError
  FAILED sklearn/frozen/tests/test_frozen.py::test_frozen_set_params_returns_self
  1 failed, 46 passed
  ```
* Green with the one-line fix: `47 passed` for `sklearn/frozen/tests/test_frozen.py`.
* No behaviour change elsewhere: `sklearn/tests/test_metaestimators.py sklearn/tests/test_base.py sklearn/frozen/tests/test_frozen.py` → `184 passed, 6 skipped` (baseline on clean `main` without the new test: `183 passed, 6 skipped`).
* `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` (pinned `ruff==0.12.2`) clean on both touched files.

The fix and the test are ready on a local branch; per the contributing guide I am not opening a PR while this issue carries the `Needs Triage` label, and I will open it (with a changelog entry) once the issue is triaged and you confirm the expected behaviour.

Related observation, **out of scope of the proposed fix**: `FrozenEstimator.fit` is declared as `fit(self, X, y, *args, **kwargs)`, so `y` is required positionally even for unsupervised frozen transformers: `FrozenEstimator(StandardScaler().fit(X)).fit(X)` raises `TypeError: FrozenEstimator.fit() missing 1 required positional argument: 'y'`, although the docstring describes `y` as ignored. `fit(X, None)` works. Happy to open a separate issue for that if you consider it a bug rather than an intentional signature.

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.12 (main, ...) [Clang ...]
executable: .../sklearn-venv/bin/python
   machine: macOS-14.5-arm64-arm-64bit

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0
          numpy: 2.5.4
          scipy: 1.18.1
```

### Introduce yourself

I want to use logistic regression in a causal setting with inverse propensity score weighting.  This is currently not possible when missing values are present.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

SimpleImputer's fit method should take the sample_weight argument.  This would enable running a pipeline like:

```Python
p = Pipeline([("imputer", SimpleImputer().set_fit_request(sample_weight=True)),
              ("lr", LogisticRegression().set_fit_request(sample_weight=True))
             ])

```

on weighted data.

### Describe your proposed solution

1. Adapt median, mean and most_frequent strategies to use weighted versions of the statistics when sample_weight is provided
2. The Callable strategy would pass sample_weight to the Callable when passed as argument to fit

title: inverse_transform of feature selectors fails when no features are selected

### Introduce yourself

Data scientist. Use scikit-learn for work.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

SelectorMixin._transform explicitly supports the case where no features are selected:
it warns "No features were selected" and returns an array of shape (n_samples, 0).
Passing that output to inverse_transform raises a ValueError instead of returning
zeros with the original number of features, as the docstring describes.
This affects SelectKBest(k=0), SelectFromModel, SelectFdr/Fpr/Fwe, etc., for both

```python
import numpy as np

y = np.array([0, 1, 0])

sel = SelectKBest(k=0).fit(X, y)
Xt = sel.transform(X)  # UserWarning: No features were selected, Xt.shape == (3, 0)
sel.inverse_transform(Xt)
```

title: BUG Sparse coordinate descent gives wrong results on a constant column without penalty

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With sparse X, a constant column and an intercept, coordinate descent can diverge or return a wrong fit when there is no penalty. The coefficients either blow up (up to ~1e288) or can stay at 0. The same fit on dense X is correct.

This affects:

- `Lasso` and `ElasticNet` with `alpha=0` and `sample_weight`. This one is in released versions, and it's more frequent on 1.9.1 (see below).
- `solver="newton-cd"` on GLMs with `alpha=0` (like `LogisticRegression`). This solver isn't released yet (new in 1.10), so we can still fix this before users hit it.

I think the impact is limited:

- It needs (almost) no penalty: `alpha=1e-16` still fails, but I saw no wrong fit from `alpha=1e-14` (or `alpha=1e-12` in logistic regression).
- All the wrong fits I saw on main came with a warning, so they aren't silent.
- The `lbfgs`, `newton-cg`, `newton-cholesky` and `newton-cd-gram` solvers are fine on the same data, and so is `Lasso` without `sample_weight`.

Constant columns in sparse matrices do happen in practice though: for instance `OneHotEncoder` produces one for a feature with a single category.

I found this through #34339, which adds sparse X to `test_glm_regression_unpenalized_hstacked_X`: its `newton-cd-csr_matrix` case fails on CI (Linux and macOS, x86-64 and arm, OpenBLAS and MKL). cc @lorentzenchr

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

The failing seeds probably depend on the platform (rounding errors), so this loops over 100 seeds:

```python
import warnings

import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, LogisticRegression, PoissonRegressor


def check(est, binary_y=False):
    n_wrong, largest_coef = 0, 0
    for seed in range(100):
        rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
        X = rng.randn(100, 3)
        y = rng.poisson(np.exp(X @ [0.3, -0.2, 0.1] + 0.5))
        y = y > 1 if binary_y else y
        X = np.c_[X, np.ones(100)]  # constant column, with fit_intercept=True
        sw = rng.lognormal(size=100)
        with warnings.catch_warnings(), np.errstate(all="ignore"):
            warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
            pred_dense = est.fit(X, y, sample_weight=sw).predict(X)
            pred_sparse = est.fit(sp.csr_array(X), y, sample_weight=sw).predict(X)
        n_wrong += not np.allclose(pred_dense, pred_sparse, rtol=1e-3)
        largest_coef = max(largest_coef, np.abs(est.coef_).max())
    print(f"{est}: wrong for {n_wrong}/100 seeds, largest |coef| {largest_coef:.1e}")


check(PoissonRegressor(alpha=0, solver="newton-cd"))
check(LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, solver="newton-cd"), binary_y=True)
check(Lasso(alpha=0))
```

Sparse and dense X give the same predictions:

```
LogisticRegression(C=inf, solver='newton-cd'): wrong for 0/100 seeds, ...
```

title: KBinsDiscretizer can produce zero bins for near-constant features, causing IndexError
description:
### Introduce yourself

Hi everyone!

I'm a B.Tech Information Technology student and I'm currently learning and contributing to open-source projects, particularly scikit-learn.

While exploring the preprocessing module and investigating the behavior of `KBinsDiscretizer`, I came across a reproducible edge case involving near-constant features. I wanted to report this because it can cause fitting or inverse transformation to fail for otherwise valid, non-constant input data.

I'm interested in understanding the underlying implementation and contributing a fix if the issue is confirmed by the maintainers.

Thank you for your time!

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`KBinsDiscretizer` can produce zero bins when a feature is non-constant but has a very small value range (`0 < max(X) - min(X) <= 1e-8`).

The constant-feature check only handles features where `col_min == col_max`. Therefore, near-constant features proceed to the binning process.

During the small-width bin filtering step in `sklearn/preprocessing/_discretization.py`, all computed intervals can be removed. This leaves only one edge and causes `n_bins_` to become zero.

This creates two user-facing failures:

1. With `encode="onehot"`, `fit()` raises an `IndexError` because an empty category array is passed to the internal encoder.
2. With `encode="ordinal"`, `fit()` and `transform()` succeed, but `inverse_transform()` raises an `IndexError` because no bin centers are available.

This affects users working with features that have very small but non-zero ranges. Such inputs should not result in an estimator state with zero bins.

I found related discussions about bins being removed, including #19416 and #25594. However, this investigation focuses specifically on the zero-bin condition and the resulting exceptions.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import KBinsDiscretizer

X = np.array([
    [1.0],
    [1.0 + 1e-10],
    [1.0 + 2e-10]
])

# One-hot encoding
kbd_onehot = KBinsDiscretizer(
    n_bins=3,
    strategy="quantile",
    encode="onehot"
)
kbd_onehot.fit(X)

# Ordinal encoding
kbd_ordinal = KBinsDiscretizer(
    n_bins=3,
    strategy="quantile",
    encode="ordinal"
)
kbd_ordinal.fit(X)

Xt = kbd_ordinal.transform(X)
kbd_ordinal.inverse_transform(Xt)
```

### Expected Results

`KBinsDiscretizer` should handle non-constant features with very small value ranges without producing zero bins.

The estimator should maintain a valid bin configuration, and `fit()`, `transform()`, and `inverse_transform()` should complete without raising unexpected `IndexError` exceptions.

Near-constant features should be handled consistently, ensuring that at least one valid bin is available.

### Actual Results

For the tested near-constant feature:

**With `encode="onehot"`:**

`fit()` raises:

```text
IndexError: index -1 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 0
```

The error occurs while fitting the internal `OneHotEncoder` with an empty category array.

**With `encode="ordinal"`:**

`fit()` succeeds, but produces:

```text
n_bins_ = array([0])
bin_edges_ = [array([1.])]
```

`transform()` returns zero for all samples.

Calling `inverse_transform()` raises:

```text
IndexError: index 0 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 0
```

The error occurs because the calculated bin centers array is empty.

The same behavior was observed with the `kmeans` strategy in the investigation.

Note: The above shows the observed exception messages. Full tracebacks and environment details should be added after final verification.

### Versions

```shell
import sklearn
sklearn.show_versions()
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would be interested in working on a pull request to resolve this issue if it is confirmed and triaged by the maintainers.

My initial investigation suggests that the issue originates in the small-width filtering logic in `KBinsDiscretizer.fit()` in `sklearn/preprocessing/_discretization.py`.

When all computed bin intervals are removed, `n_bins_` becomes zero. A possible approach would be to handle this edge case explicitly and ensure that a valid bin configuration is retained for near-constant features.

I would also add regression tests covering both `quantile` and `kmeans` strategies, as well as `onehot` and `ordinal` encodings, including `inverse_transform()`.

I will wait for maintainer feedback before preparing a pull request.

title: HTML repr: keyboard focus is invisible on the expand/collapse toggles (WCAG 2.4.7)
description: > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. I'm Eya, a full-stack developer with a Research Master's in ICT. I use scikit-learn in my machine learning work and I'm interested in the accessibility of its HTML displays. I recently reported and fixed a similar accessibility issue in skrub's TableReport (skrub-data/skrub#2389). This is my first issue on scikit-learn. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact When navigating the estimator HTML representation with the keyboard (Tab), focus lands on the expand/collapse toggles of each step, but nothing on screen shows where the focus is. The focused element is the hidden checkbox `input.sk-toggleable__control.sk-hidden--visually` (rendered at 1×1 px), and its associated `label.sk-toggleable__label` gets no visible style when the input is focused. Pressing Space does toggle the step, so the control is operable, but a keyboard user cannot see which step they are about to open. The `?` documentation links already show a focus outline, so the issue is only on the toggles. This fails WCAG 2.1 success criterion 2.4.7 (Focus Visible). Since the HTML repr is displayed throughout the documentation, this may also be relevant to the accessibility audit in #31965. A possible fix is a CSS rule such as `.sk-toggleable__control:focus-visible + label { outline: 2px solid ...; outline-offset: 2px; }` I would be glad to help with a pull request if that is useful. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor from sklearn.utils import estimator_html_repr pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), HistGradientBoostingRegressor()) with open("pipe.html", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: f.write(estimator_html_repr(pipe)) # Open pipe.html in a browser, click on the page, then press Tab twice. ### Expected Results The focused toggle shows a visible focus indicator (for example an outline around its label), as the `?` documentation links already do. ### Actual Results Focus moves to the toggle (Space opens/closes it), but no visual change appears, so the keyboard user cannot tell which step is focused. The screenshot below shows the page after pressing Tab: no step is highlighted, while a DevTools live expression confirms that `document.activeElement` is the hidden toggle input. ### Versions ```shell import sklearn; sklearn.show_versions() ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes, I would be glad to open a pull request with the CSS fix and a before/after screenshot, if the maintainers (and the team working on the accessibility audit in #31965) agree with the approach.

title: LinearDiscriminantAnalysis: "svd" and "lsqr"/"eigen" solvers disagree when priors differ from class proportions
description:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a senior data scientist and I use scikit-learn regularly for classification and modelling work. I found this while checking that the three LDA solvers give the same results as the closed-form Gaussian model. I used AI tools to help me investigate and write this report, and I reproduced the bug myself on main.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When `priors` differs from the class proportions in `y`, `LinearDiscriminantAnalysis` gives different `predict_proba` and `predict` results depending on the solver.

The cause is how the within-class covariance is weighted:
- `solver="svd"` (the default) weights each class covariance by its sample count: `sum_k (n_k / n) * C_k`.
- `solver="lsqr"` and `solver="eigen"` weight by the priors: `sum_k prior_k * C_k`, which is also how `covariance_` is documented. With `store_covariance=True`, the svd solver reports this prior-weighted `covariance_` but does not predict with it.

With `priors=None` the two weightings are identical, so the solvers agree.

Impact: setting balanced priors on imbalanced data is a common use of `priors`. Then the predictions depend on the solver, and switching solver (e.g. to use shrinkage, which "svd" does not support) silently changes them. In the example below, about 15% of the predicted labels change.

#33626 already made the solvers agree for the default priors; this is the case it does not cover.

Which weighting is intended? Weighting by class counts is the maximum likelihood estimate of the shared covariance (the priors then only enter through the log(prior_k) term), while the documentation of `covariance_` describes prior weighting.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
# 200 vs 20 samples, classes with different spread
X = np.vstack([rng.randn(200, 2) * [1.0, 0.3], rng.randn(20, 2) * [0.3, 2.0] + [1.5, 0.5]])
y = np.repeat([0, 1], [200, 20])
X_test = rng.uniform(-3, 3, size=(2000, 2))

lda = {
    solver: LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(
        solver=solver, priors=[0.5, 0.5], store_covariance=True
    ).fit(X, y)
    for solver in ["svd", "lsqr", "eigen"]
}
proba = {s: m.predict_proba(X_test) for s, m in lda.items()}
pred = {s: m.predict(X_test) for s, m in lda.items()}

print("same covariance_ for svd and lsqr:", np.allclose(lda["svd"].covariance_, lda["lsqr"].covariance_))
print("max |proba svd - proba lsqr|:", np.abs(proba["svd"] - proba["lsqr"]).max())
print("max |proba eigen - proba lsqr|:", np.abs(proba["eigen"] - proba["lsqr"]).max())
print("labels differing, svd vs lsqr:", (pred["svd"] != pred["lsqr"]).mean())
```

### Expected Results

All three solvers give the same probabilities and labels (up to floating point error), as they do with `priors=None`.

### Actual Results

```
max |proba svd - proba lsqr|: 0.7918808064805439
max |proba eigen - proba lsqr|: 4.440892098500626e-16
labels differing, svd vs lsqr: 0.1455
```

### Introduce yourself

Hello,

I am Fatih Aydın, a faculty member in the Department of Computer Engineering at Balıkesir University.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The FAQ page mentions that projects compatible with scikit-learn can be listed on the "Related Projects" page. Therefore, I would like to propose adding the `scikit-reduce` package—which I developed—to this page.

Repository: https://github.com/fatihaydin1/scikit-reduce

The package currently includes two methods, both of which I authored:

- NIS (Nimble Instance Selection): A fast, label-free instance selection method. It implements the `fit_resample` interface and can be used within `imbalanced-learn` pipelines (Neural Computing and Applications, 2023).
- BLDOD (Boundary-aware Local Density-based Outlier Detection): An outlier detection method that follows the scikit-learn outlier detection interface (`fit`, `score_samples`, `decision_function`, `predict`) (Information Sciences, 2023).

Both estimators pass the `check_estimator` tests. The tests are run via GitHub Actions on Linux, Windows, and macOS, using scikit-learn 1.6 and the latest version. The package is licensed under the MIT license.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

The "Other estimators and tasks → Pre-processing" section on the page seems appropriate, especially since `imbalanced-learn` is also listed there. The entry to be added could look like this:

`scikit-reduce`: Instance selection (NIS) and outlier detection (BLDOD) methods with scikit-learn-compatible interfaces.

If you find this suitable, I can submit a pull request (PR) to add this line to the `doc/related_projects.rst` file.

For the sake of transparency, I should mention that the package code was written with the assistance of an AI coding assistant; I have reviewed and verified the code myself. The outputs were verified by comparing them against my original MATLAB implementations using GNU Octave: it selects the same samples for the NIS 55 dataset and yields the same scores for the BLDOD 17 dataset. The comparison scripts can be found in the repository under the `tools/verify_reference` folder.

Thanks,
Fatih Aydın

title: RFC Array API support for `KMeans` and its `"kmeans++"` inititialization
description:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

I prototyped some array API support for `KMeans` with the help of a coding agent. I did that by iteratively running experiments and logging results in an HTML journal maintained in an branch of an external repo that I dedicate to de-novo experiments:

- https://github.com/ogrisel/cursor-sandbox/pull/17

The descriptions of the repo has an up to date detailed summary of what was explored. There are even more details with experimentation results and plots in the [agent's managed journal](https://ogrisel.github.io/cursor-sandbox/pr-17/) but the journal entries are iterative and therefore harder to interpret than the high level summary in the linked PR's description.

### Main results

- on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU, a generic array API implementation of kmeans++ and Lloyd iterations can be competitive with cuML and both can be much faster (up to 7x) than the best CPU implementation on that AWS host;
- the same array API code on CPU is not competitive with our existing Cython implementation and even less so when taking optimizations proposed by @cakedev0 (in particular https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/35140) into account;
- I also explored Torch- and CuPy-specific optimizations on top of the generic array API code path: those can improve performance a bit for some cases (large numbers of clusters) with moderate added complexity.

### My take

- I think I would be in favor of expanding our KMeans class to include a array API codepath for non-NumPy inputs, in particular to leverage the capabilities non-CPU devices.
- I don't think it's worth bothering with the Torch and CuPy specific codepaths in a first PR. Making a decision about backend specific array API code branches should be discussed in follow-up issues and PRs if people feel the need for them.
- I think we should keep the Cython codepath for the CPU case. It means that we will have a bit of code duplication to maintain but I think it's ok. It's similar to what we have for the Cython/array API optimized loss module used by linear models with array API support.
- I observed that CuPy is a bit slower than PyTorch CUDA (1.1x to 2.x slower depending on the data and number of clusters).

### Limitations

I have not experimented with the multiple GPU setting. I think the "scalable-kmeans++" init of cuML would make it harder for a simple array API implementation to be competitive in that more advanced setting.

title: BUG: metrics.auc returns incorrect areas for decreasing unsigned coordinates and fails monotonicity validation
description:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Saurav Singla, a Head of Data Science working on machine learning and model evaluation.

While investigating metric correctness with AI assistance, I found that `sklearn.metrics.auc` can silently return an incorrect area when decreasing x-coordinates are stored as unsigned integers. The investigation reproduced this behavior in scikit-learn 1.7.2, 1.8.0, and 1.9.1. Equivalent floating-point inputs produce the expected result.

I’m reporting this because decreasing coordinates are explicitly supported by the documentation, and unsigned inputs also appear to bypass the monotonicity check. I could not find an existing scikit-learn issue describing this specific behavior. I’ve included a minimal reproducer and environment details below.


### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`sklearn.metrics.auc` silently computes incorrect areas when decreasing x-coordinates are stored as unsigned integers, although decreasing coordinates are explicitly supported by its documentation.

For example, with `x = np.array([2, 1, 0], dtype=np.uint8)` and `y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0])`, the expected area is `1.0`, but `auc(x, y)` returns `255.0` without a warning. Converting the same coordinates to `float64`, or reversing both arrays, returns `1.0`.

Unsigned inputs also bypass monotonicity validation: `x = np.array([0, 2, 1], dtype=np.uint8)` returns a numeric result, whereas the equivalent floating-point input raises `ValueError`.

I encountered this during a targeted investigation of metric correctness with AI assistance, rather than through a production incident. I care about evaluation results being consistent across equivalent numeric representations. For users passing unsigned coordinate arrays directly to `auc`, the behavior can silently corrupt reported areas and allow invalid curves through validation.

The behavior was reproduced in scikit-learn 1.7.2, 1.8.0, and 1.9.1. This report concerns direct calls to `auc`; it does not demonstrate a problem with ordinary `roc_auc_score` usage.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.metrics import auc

print("scikit-learn:", sklearn.__version__)

y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0])

# Valid decreasing coordinates: all three results should be 1.0.
x = np.array([2, 1, 0], dtype=np.uint8)
print("Unsigned:", auc(x, y))                         # 255.0
print("Float:", auc(x.astype(np.float64), y))         # 1.0
print("Reversed:", auc(x[::-1], y[::-1]))              # 1.0

# Non-monotonic coordinates: both calls should raise ValueError.
for dtype in (np.uint8, np.float64):
    x = np.array([0, 2, 1], dtype=dtype)
    try:
        print(f"{dtype.__name__}, non-monotonic:", auc(x, y))
    except ValueError:
        print(f"{dtype.__name__}, non-monotonic: ValueError")

### Expected Results

For the valid decreasing coordinates, all three representations should return `1.0`. Converting the coordinates from unsigned integers to floats, or reversing both arrays, should not change the area.

For the non-monotonic coordinates `[0, 2, 1]`, both unsigned integer and floating-point inputs should raise `ValueError`.

Expected output, excluding the version line:

```text
Unsigned: 1.0
Float: 1.0
Reversed: 1.0
uint8, non-monotonic: ValueError
float64, non-monotonic: ValueError
```


### Actual Results

Observed output on scikit-learn 1.9.1:

```text
scikit-learn: 1.9.1
Unsigned: 255.0
Float: 1.0
Reversed: 1.0
uint8, non-monotonic: 128.5
float64, non-monotonic: ValueError
```

The decreasing unsigned coordinates produce `255.0` instead of `1.0`. The non-monotonic unsigned coordinates return `128.5` instead of raising `ValueError`.

Both incorrect unsigned-input results are returned silently, without a warning or exception, so there is no traceback for the reported failures. The `ValueError` for the floating-point control is expected and caught by the reproducer.

The same results were also reproduced on scikit-learn 1.7.2 and 1.8.0, using NumPy 2.3.5 and SciPy 1.17.0.


### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.14 (main, Aug 25 2026, 14:00:49) [Clang 22.1.3 ]
executable: /opt/codex/runtimes/codex-primary-runtime/dependencies/python/bin/python
   machine: Linux-6.18.55-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.1
          pip: 26.2.2
   setuptools: 84.1.0
        numpy: 2.3.5
        scipy: 1.17.0
       Cython: None
       pandas: 2.2.3
   matplotlib: 3.10.8
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.27.1

Built with OpenMP: True

threadpoolctl info:
       user_api: blas
   internal_api: openblas
    num_threads: 9
         prefix: libscipy_openblas
       filepath: /opt/codex/runtimes/codex-primary-runtime/dependencies/python/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-fdde5778.so
        version: 0.3.30
threading_layer: pthreads
   architecture: SkylakeX

       user_api: blas
   internal_api: openblas
    num_threads: 9
         prefix: libscipy_openblas
       filepath: /opt/codex/runtimes/codex-primary-runtime/dependencies/python/lib/python3.12/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-6cdc3b4a.so
        version: 0.3.30
threading_layer: pthreads
   architecture: SkylakeX

       user_api: openmp
   internal_api: openmp
    num_threads: 9
         prefix: libgomp
       filepath: /tmp/sklearn191/scikit_learn.libs/libgomp-e985bcbb.so.1.0.0
        version: None
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would be interested in working on a PR after maintainers confirm and triage the issue, with AI assistance disclosed.

The apparent root cause is that `auc` uses `np.diff(x)` to determine direction and validate monotonicity. For unsigned inputs, decreasing differences wrap to positive values, so these checks fail. The subsequent trapezoidal integration also performs subtraction on the unsigned coordinates.

A possible fix would:

* Determine monotonicity and direction using direct comparisons between adjacent coordinates, avoiding subtraction.
* Ensure coordinate differences used for integration are computed safely.
* Add regression tests for decreasing and non-monotonic inputs across unsigned integer types, with signed integer and floating-point controls.

The dtype strategy needs care: blindly converting `uint64` to `int64` can overflow, while converting to `float64` can lose precision for large integers. I would discuss the preferred handling with maintainers before implementing it.

I will wait for triage before opening a PR.

title: Categorical trees: error message and docstring state the wrong limit for categorical_features
description:
### Describe the bug

With the new native categorical support in trees (#33354, #33972, forests in #34832), the input values get ordinal-encoded internally before validation, so the raw category values can be anything (negative, non-integer, > 255). The real limit is on the **number** of distinct categories, and it's 256 (not 255) with `splitter="best"`.

But the docstring and error message still describe the older "codes must already be in [0, 255]" design:

- the `categorical_features` docstring (`DecisionTreeClassifier`, `DecisionTreeRegressor` and the forests) says "at most 255 unique categories", but 256 work fine (all 256 predicted correctly, also with missing values present)
- with 257+ categories the error says `Values for categorical features should be integers in [0, 255]. Found 256.` even when my values are e.g. `1000..1256`. The `256` is the internal encoded max (`n_cats - 1`), not something from my data, so the message points at the wrong problem
- same wording for `splitter="random"`: `integers in [0, 16777215]`

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

# 1. values outside [0, 255], negative and non-integer values are all accepted
X = np.array([[-1.0], [0.5], [300.0], [2000.0]] * 10)
y = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] * 10)
tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(categorical_features=[0]).fit(X, y)
print(tree.predict([[-1.0], [0.5], [300.0], [2000.0]]))

# 2. 256 unique categories are accepted (docstring says at most 255)
X = np.arange(256, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)
DecisionTreeRegressor(categorical_features=[0]).fit(X, np.arange(256.0))
print("256 categories: fitted")

# 3. 257 unique categories: the error talks about the value range
X = np.arange(1000, 1257, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)
DecisionTreeRegressor(categorical_features=[0]).fit(X, np.arange(257.0))
```

### Expected Results

- the docstring states the real limit (256 categories with `splitter="best"`)
- the error describes the actual problem, e.g. `Categorical feature 0 has 257 categories, but at most 256 are supported with splitter="best".`

### Actual Results

```
[1. 2. 3. 4.]
256 categories: fitted
ValueError: Values for categorical features should be integers in [0, 255]. Found 256.
```

### Additional context

I think this comes from the first version of #33354, where the codes had to be "contiguous integers in [0, 255]". The ordinal encoding was added later, but the message and docstring weren't updated. #35181 moves this check but keeps the same message, so cc @cakedev0. Happy to open a PR for it, either after #35181 or folded into it, whichever you prefer.

### Versions

```
sklearn: 1.10.dev0 (nightly wheel, main @ 59106029d)
python: 3.12.4, Windows 11
numpy: 2.6.0.dev0, scipy: 2.0.0.dev0, pandas: 3.2.0.dev0
narwhals: 2.27.1, joblib: 1.6.0, threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
```

### Introduce yourself

I am a reseacher, using ML for neuroimaging/cognitive neuroscience. I'm one of the core-developers of a library we used at then INM-7, in Forschungszentrum Jülich, which is heaviliy based on scikit-learn.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

We usually work with complex ensemble/meta models, like StackingClassifier/Regressor. In one of our tests, we detected that the `Pipeline.score` function, with metadata routing, is passing `sample_weight` unconditionally. If the pipeline ends with a StackingRegressor (e.g.), and the `sample_weight` is not needed, this raises an error.

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = make_regression(random_state=0)
pipe = make_pipeline(StackingRegressor([("lr", LinearRegression())])).fit(X, y)
pipe.score(X, y)

title: Add `reliability_curve` and `ReliabilityDisplay` for regressors
description:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I'd like to move forward with adding a reliability curve and display class for regressors.
This has been agreed upon as a follow-up topic in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34261#issuecomment-5003606483 (I don't intend to address the `reliability_error` part here, which will be a topic of its own, but I think the curve and display can be added independent of that).
It was also previously noted as desirable to have in B.1. in issue https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/21718.

This can then also be used in [this example](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/auto_examples/linear_model/plot_poisson_regression_non_normal_loss.html#evaluation-of-the-calibration-of-predictions).

As discussed with @ogrisel, it could also be extended to support quantile regression, possibly implemented as a `kwarg` variation in a follow-up, which can then be used to simplify https://github.com/soda-inria/tabicl/pull/75.

### Describe your proposed solution

I would start with implementing `reliability_curve` and `ReliabilityDisplay` for mean regression, similar to the calibration counterparts we already have for classification.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

There will be overlap with the calibration counterparts, but as was already discussed in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34261#issuecomment-4842348096, `calibration_curve` (and `CalibrationDisplay`) are classifier specific and 
>retro-fitting it to accommodate regressions would make the signature a little funky

so https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34261#issuecomment-4981601962 suggested to use separate implementations and the `reliability` terminology for the regression case.

### Additional context

@lorentzenchr's [model-diagnostics](https://github.com/lorentzenchr/model-diagnostics) implements `plot_reliability_diagram` using isotonic regression, which has also been proposed for classification in #23132 and #23824. From what I understand, this can also be used as `strategy` for regression. I'd start from the recently updated default values of `calibration_curve` (`n_bins=cube_root` and `startegy=quantile`), and leave this as a follow-up.

title: BUG: MinMaxScaler and MaxAbsScaler partial_fit produce NaN statistics after an all-NaN batch
description:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Rugved, an AI Engineer Intern and machine-learning practitioner. I use scikit-learn for preprocessing, model training, evaluation, and practical machine-learning projects.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

While investigating incremental preprocessing with missing values, I found that `MinMaxScaler.partial_fit()` and `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` can discard valid statistics learned from earlier batches.

If a feature contains valid values in one batch but only NaN values in a later batch, the later batch replaces the feature's accumulated statistics with NaN.

This affects users processing large or streaming datasets in batches. A batch with no valid observations for a feature should not invalidate statistics already learned for that feature. Currently, subsequent transformations of finite values in that feature also produce NaN.

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, MaxAbsScaler

print("scikit-learn:", sklearn.__version__)

A = np.array([
    [1.0, 10.0],
    [3.0, 20.0],
])

B = np.array([
    [np.nan, 30.0],
    [np.nan, 40.0],
])

X = np.vstack([A, B])

for cls in (MinMaxScaler, MaxAbsScaler):
    batch_scaler = cls().fit(X)

    incremental_scaler = cls().partial_fit(A)
    incremental_scaler.partial_fit(B)

    print(f"\n{cls.__name__}")

    for attr in ("data_min_", "data_max_", "max_abs_", "scale_"):
        if hasattr(incremental_scaler, attr):
            print(f"{attr}: {getattr(incremental_scaler, attr)}")

    print(
        "Incremental transform:",
        incremental_scaler.transform([[2.0, 25.0]])
    )

    print(
        "Batch-fit transform:",
        batch_scaler.transform([[2.0, 25.0]])
    )
```

### Expected Results

The all-NaN values in the first feature of the second batch should be treated as missing and ignored during the incremental update.

Previously learned valid statistics should be preserved. The incremental results should match fitting on the combined dataset.

For the example above:

```text
MinMaxScaler:
data_min_: [1. 10.]
data_max_: [3. 40.]
scale_: [0.5        0.03333333]
Incremental transform: [[0.5 0.5]]

MaxAbsScaler:
max_abs_: [ 3. 40.]
scale_: [ 3. 40.]
Incremental transform: [[0.66666667 0.625]]
```

Finite input values should not be transformed to NaN merely because a later batch contains no valid observations for that feature.

### Actual Results

The second `partial_fit` call completes without raising an exception, but it corrupts the statistics for the first feature.

Observed output with scikit-learn 1.6.1:

```text
MinMaxScaler
data_min_: [nan 10.]
data_max_: [nan 40.]
scale_: [       nan 0.03333333]
Incremental transform: [[nan 0.5]]
Batch-fit transform: [[0.5 0.5]]

MaxAbsScaler
max_abs_: [nan 40.]
scale_: [nan 40.]
Incremental transform: [[  nan 0.625]]
Batch-fit transform: [[0.66666667 0.625     ]]
```

The update also emits:

```text
RuntimeWarning: All-NaN slice encountered
```

No exception is raised, but finite values in the affected feature are transformed to NaN.

### Versions

- Python: 3.12.13
- scikit-learn: 1.6.1
- NumPy: 2.0.2
- SciPy: 1.16.3
- Runtime: Linux x86_64

### Additional Context

The documentation for both scalers states that NaNs are treated as missing values and disregarded during fitting.

A related issue involving the same pattern in `StandardScaler.partial_fit()` is [#35070](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/35070).

### Interest in Fixing the Bug

Yes, I would be interested in working on a PR if the issue is confirmed and triaged by the maintainers.

The apparent root cause is in the incremental aggregation logic. For an all-NaN feature, the per-batch statistic is NaN:

- `MinMaxScaler` computes `nanmin` and `nanmax`, which return NaN for an all-NaN feature.
- `MaxAbsScaler` computes the maximum absolute value, which also returns NaN for an all-NaN feature.

During subsequent `partial_fit` calls, these NaN batch statistics are merged with the previously stored statistics using ordinary minimum/maximum operations. Those operations propagate NaN and overwrite valid statistics.

A possible fix would be to merge statistics while treating a NaN batch statistic as “no new observation”:

- If the previous statistic is valid and the new batch statistic is NaN, preserve the previous value.
- If the previous statistic is NaN and the new batch statistic is valid, use the new value.
- If both values are NaN, preserve NaN because no valid observation has been seen.

I would add regression tests covering both scalers, including comparisons between incremental fitting and fitting on the combined dataset. I would wait for maintainer feedback on the intended behavior and edge cases before opening a PR.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

```python
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
```

title: BUG `GridSearchCV(n_jobs=8)` is 10x to 50x slower than in 1.8 on many small tasks: every task pickles the whole callback context tree
description:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Since the callbacks API (#33322), a parallel `GridSearchCV` with many cheap fits is much slower than in 1.8. On a 2000-candidate grid on iris (10k fits of ~1 ms), `n_jobs=8` takes ~3 s on 1.8.0 but 100-150 s on 1.9.1 and 24-67 s on main. That's much slower than `n_jobs=1` (~9 s). No callback is registered.

`BaseSearchCV.fit` creates one `CallbackContext` per (candidate, split) up front and passes one to each `_fit_and_score` task. `subcontext` registers the child in the parent's `_children_map` and sets `child.parent`, so pickling one task's context pickles its parent and every sibling. The pickled task grows linearly with the number of tasks: ~50 KB per task for 500 tasks, ~420 KB per task for 5000 tasks (measured on main by pickling the `delayed` arguments `BaseSearchCV.fit` builds).

joblib pickles each batch separately, so the total pickling work is roughly (number of batches) x (number of tasks). Auto-batching hides part of it because a batch shares the pickle memo. With `pre_dispatch="all"` (batches of one task) and `refit=False`, the search takes 290 s on main, and 4.6 s with the contexts left out of the tasks.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import time

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
param_grid = {"max_depth": range(1, 21), "random_state": range(100)}  # 2000 candidates

for n_jobs in [1, 8]:
    search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(), param_grid, cv=5, n_jobs=n_jobs)
    tic = time.perf_counter()
    search.fit(X, y)
    print(f"n_jobs={n_jobs}: {time.perf_counter() - tic:.1f}s")
```

### Expected Results

Same as 1.8.0:

```
n_jobs=1: 8.7s
n_jobs=8: 3.1s
```

### Actual Results

1.9.1:

```
n_jobs=1: 10.9s
n_jobs=8: 105.9s
```

`n_jobs=8` varies a lot between runs: 100.6 s, 105.9 s and 151.1 s on 1.9.1, and 23.8 s, 31.9 s and 67.2 s on main. 1.8.0 is stable at 3.0-3.1 s. Intel Core Ultra 5 225H (14 cores), same Python and joblib for all three.

_No response_

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

We use Isotonic regression to calibrate scores on a log-odds / log-likelihood-ratio scale. On such scales, the extreme values are naturally +inf / -inf (e.g., probabilities of exactly 0 or 1). IsotonicRegression.fit currently rejects these inputs:
```
import numpy as np
```

_No response_

title: BUG: thread-based `Parallel` can corrupt the process-wide warning filters
description:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

On Python without context-aware warnings (every GIL build, and free-threaded 3.13), `sklearn.utils.parallel.Parallel` with a thread-based backend can corrupt the process-wide warning filters. The user's own filters can be silently lost, and spurious "`sklearn.utils.parallel.delayed` should be used with `sklearn.utils.parallel.Parallel`" warnings are raised.

To propagate the caller's warning filters to joblib workers (#30380), every task runs:

```python
with warnings.catch_warnings():  # save the global filter list, swap in a copy
    warnings.resetwarnings()  # empty it
    for f in captured_filters:  # re-add the caller's filters one by one
        warnings.filterwarnings(...)
    return func(*args, **kwargs)
# on exit: restore the saved list
```

Without context-aware warnings, `warnings.filters` is one list shared by the whole process, and `catch_warnings` isn't thread-safe (the Python docs say so). With threads, tasks enter and exit these blocks out of order:

1. Thread 1 enters: it saves the user's list (L0), the global becomes a copy (L1), and it starts emptying and refilling L1.
2. Thread 2 enters while L1 is half-refilled: it saves L1, the global becomes L2.
3. Thread 1 exits and restores L0.
4. Thread 2 exits and restores L1: the half-reset copy.

A task's `resetwarnings()` can also run while the global list is the very list captured by `Parallel` (after another thread restored it), and empty it: the next tasks then see no filters and raise the warning above.

It needs a thread switch at the wrong moment, so it's rare with the default switch interval (5 ms) and a few threads. It's more frequent with many threads, with `catch_warnings` calls inside the tasks (`check_array` and `get_params` do that), and when tests run in several threads at once: I think this is the intermittent failure of #32631 on free-threaded 3.13, xfailed in #33320.

On free-threaded 3.14 (context-aware warnings) there is no race, but the same code takes the `warnings` module lock in every task, which makes many threads queue on it.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import sys
import warnings

from sklearn.utils.parallel import Parallel, delayed

sys.setswitchinterval(1e-5)  # makes the race frequent

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="my filter")
n_before = len(warnings.filters)
for _ in range(3):
    Parallel(n_jobs=32, prefer="threads")(delayed(int)() for _ in range(200))

my_filter_kept = any(f[1] is not None and f[1].pattern == "my filter" for f in warnings.filters)
print(f"{n_before} -> {len(warnings.filters)} filters, my filter kept: {my_filter_kept}")
```

### Expected Results

```
11 -> 11 filters, my filter kept: True
```

and no warning.

### Actual Results

On every run (3 runs, GIL 3.14.7, 344-thread machine):

```
11 -> 0 filters, my filter kept: False
```

and 88 to 172 spurious warnings per run:

```
sklearn/utils/parallel.py:144: UserWarning: `sklearn.utils.parallel.delayed` should be used with `sklearn.utils.parallel.Parallel` to make it possible to propagate the scikit-learn configuration of the current thread to the joblib workers.
```

On a 14-core laptop (GIL 3.14.6) it happens as well, for instance `11 -> 4 filters` with hundreds of warnings.

title: BUG: StandardScaler.partial_fit replaces an existing variance with NaN when a new dense batch has an all-NaN feature
description:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm exploring numerical reliability in scientific Python through AI-assisted investigation and testing.
This issue came from checking how StandardScaler.partial_fit handles batches with missing observations and comparing incremental results with batch fitting.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

After StandardScaler learns valid statistics for a feature, a subsequent dense batch containing only NaNs in that feature changes its var_ and scale_ to NaN, while its mean_ and sample count remain correct.

In the recorded checks, this also causes finite values in that feature to be transformed to NaN.

The StandardScaler documentation states that NaNs are treated as missing values and disregarded during fitting. The example below supplies no new valid observations for the first feature.

Documentation:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler.html

Related work:
PR #16466 included preserving sparse incremental statistics when a new batch contributes zero valid observations, including all-NaN second-batch tests. This report concerns the dense-array counterpart.
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/16466

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

A = np.array([[1., 10.], [3., 20.]])
B = np.array([[np.nan, 30.], [np.nan, 40.]])

scaler = StandardScaler()
scaler.partial_fit(A)
np.testing.assert_allclose(scaler.var_, [1., 25.])

scaler.partial_fit(B)
np.testing.assert_allclose(scaler.var_[0], 1.)
```

### Expected Results

The final assertion should pass. After processing B, the first feature should retain its mean of 2, variance of 1, scale of 1, and sample count of 2, because B contains no new non-missing observations for that feature.

The second feature should have a mean of 25, variance of 125, scale of sqrt(125), and sample count of 4.

### Actual Results

title: ENH Ridge: support `solver="cholesky"` for array API inputs
description:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

Credit to @ogrisel for the idea.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

With array API dispatch, `Ridge` only supports `solver="svd"`, and `solver="auto"` resolves to `"svd"` with a warning (#27800 started with SVD only). The SVD is much more expensive than the Cholesky path used for NumPy inputs, so `Ridge` on GPU is often slower than `Ridge` on CPU with NumPy, and sometimes much slower.

I'd like `solver="cholesky"` (and so `solver="auto"`) to work with array API inputs, and be fast on GPU.

### Describe your proposed solution

Split the Cholesky solver in two: compute the Gram matrix on the device (`X.T @ X`, or `X @ X.T` in the dual case when `n_features > n_samples`), move it to the host, and solve it with the existing NumPy/SciPy code. Then move the coefficients back to the device:

```python
def _solve_cholesky_array_api(X, y, alpha, xp):
    n_samples, n_features = X.shape
    dual = n_features > n_samples
    G = X @ X.T if dual else X.T @ X  # the expensive part, on the device
    rhs = y if dual else X.T @ y
    G, rhs = _convert_to_numpy(G, xp), _convert_to_numpy(rhs, xp)
    # same solve as for NumPy inputs: scipy.linalg.solve(..., assume_a="pos")
    if dual:
        coef = _solve_cholesky_kernel(G, rhs, alpha)
    else:
        coef = _solve_cholesky_gram(G, rhs, alpha)  # _solve_cholesky, minus the Gram matrix
    coef = xp.asarray(coef, device=device(X))
    if dual:
        coef = X.T @ coef
    return coef
```

Let's call this policy A. The system to solve is only `(n_features, n_features)` (or `(n_samples, n_samples)`), so the host solve and the transfers are cheap compared to the Gram matrix. And the solve behaves exactly like for NumPy inputs, whatever the namespace: same SPD solver, same `LinAlgError` handling for singular systems.

`solver="auto"` could then resolve to `"cholesky"` for array API inputs, like for NumPy inputs, and the warning would go away.

I prototyped it by swapping `_solve_svd` during `Ridge.fit` (`fit_intercept=True`, `alpha=1.0`, one target, standard normal data, best of 3 after a warmup, torch 2.13). Coefficients match the NumPy Cholesky solver to ~1e-6 in float32 and ~1e-14 in float64. Fit times in seconds, policy B is the fully on-device alternative described below:

NVIDIA L4, NumPy on 8 vCPUs (AMD EPYC 7R13):

| shape | dtype | NumPy cholesky | torch svd (current) | policy A | policy B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 500,000 x 100 | float32 | 0.13 | 0.091 | 0.011 | 0.011 |
| 500,000 x 100 | float64 | 0.20 | 0.45 | 0.059 | 0.059 |
| 50,000 x 1000 | float32 | 0.27 | 0.21 | 0.024 | 0.018 |
| 50,000 x 1000 | float64 | 0.44 | 2.3 | 0.29 | 0.28 |
| 463,810 x 990 | float32 | 1.9 | not run | 0.15 | 0.15 |
| 463,810 x 990 | float64 | 3.6 | not run | 2.5 | 2.5 |
| 2,500 x 20,000 | float32 | 0.52 | 1.5 | 0.12 | 0.044 |
| 2,500 x 20,000 | float64 | 0.93 | 13 | 0.80 | 0.69 |
| 5,000 x 40,000 | float32 | 3.1 | not run | 0.66 | 0.27 |

Intel Arc B390 iGPU (Panther Lake), NumPy on the 16 cores of the Core Ultra X7 358H:

| shape | dtype | NumPy cholesky | torch svd (current) | policy A | policy B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 500,000 x 100 | float32 | 0.12 | 0.49 | 0.021 | 0.021 |
| 50,000 x 1000 | float32 | 0.14 | 1.1 | 0.037 | 0.036 |
| 50,000 x 1000 | float64 | 0.35 | 2.0 | 0.27 | 0.27 |
| 463,810 x 990 | float32 | 1.1 | not run | 0.30 | 0.30 |
| 2,500 x 20,000 | float32 | 0.27 | 10 | 0.11 | 0.075 |
| 2,500 x 20,000 | float64 | 0.66 | 17 | 0.79 | 0.71 |
| 5,000 x 40,000 | float32 | 2.5 | not run | 0.85 | 0.74 |

Policy A is 7x to 90x faster than the current SVD, and in float32 2.5x to 13x faster than NumPy on CPU. In float64, with ~1000 features or more, it is only 0.8x to 1.5x the speed of NumPy: both GPUs have a low float64 throughput (~450 GFLOP/s measured on the Arc B390), and the Gram matrix is a float64 matmul.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Policy B: solve on the device with `xp.linalg.solve`, which is in the array API `linalg` extension.

It is faster than policy A only when the system to solve is large, in practice in the dual case: up to 2.7x in float32 on the L4. Elsewhere both are within noise, because the Gram matrix dominates.

But each namespace handles the solve its own way, and checking them all is hard. For instance, on a singular system `torch.linalg.solve` raises a `_LinAlgError`, while `cupy.linalg.solve` returns NaNs by default. Some namespaces may also not implement the `linalg` extension. Policy A avoids all of this by reusing the code path we already test with NumPy.

### Additional context

#34793 (centering trick for the Cholesky solver) would help here too: it avoids the centered copy of `X`, which halves the device memory needed by `fit`.

I'd go with policy A. We could switch the solve to the device later for large systems if it turns out to matter.
